findings.claim: US imports under HS 8504 reached about $35.4B in 2025, up from $16.1B in 2020.
findings.detail: CPA analysis of Census data. HS 8504 is dominated by static converters and power supplies (8504.40), so this overstates the transformer market. The baseline had no 2025 total. Computed 2023 total for comparison: ~$28.7B (Mexico $5.74B ÷ 20% share, TrendEconomy).

findings.claim: China's share of US HS 8504 imports fell from about 27% in 2020 to about 10% ($3.6B) in 2025.
findings.detail: Cross-check: Trading Economics/UN Comtrade lists US imports from China of HS 8504 at $3.63B (2025) and $4.0B (2024), and TrendEconomy gives $4.27B (2023). China-reported exports to the US in 2024 were $4.67B; mirror gaps are normal.

findings.claim: Mexico supplied about $5.74B of US HS 8504 imports in 2023 (20% share), $6.18B in 2024 and about $6.3B in 2025, so the baseline's '~$2.3B in 2023, ~20% of HS 8504' mixes two scopes.
findings.detail: Sources: 2023 from TrendEconomy (Comtrade); 2024 from Trading Economics (https://tradingeconomics.com/united-states/imports/mexico/electrical-electronic-equipment); 2025 from CPA. The baseline's $2.3B matches IndexBox's narrower 'electrical transformers' scope (Mexico $2,339M in 2023), but the 20% share belongs to the full HS 8504 heading. Both readings should be stated separately.
findings.verify_evidence: I could not verify this independently. My first four WebSearch calls (TrendEconomy, Trading Economics, nextmsc, Korea Customs) all came back unexecuted because this turn's shared 200-search budget was already used up. Checks I could run: (1) The baseline does mix scopes in the way described. dashboard/build_data.py line 48 attributes both '$2.3B' and 'about 20% of HS 8504 imports' to a single IndexBox page (indexbox.io/blog/us-electrical-transformer-imports-2023). So the critique holds as a description of the baseline. (2) The 2024 figure ($6.18B) is cited to tradingeconomics.com/.../imports/mexico/electrical-electronic-equipment. That URL slug is the HS chapter 85 page, not HS 8504. Unless the researcher pulled an HS 8504 sub-line from that page, $6.18B may not be HS 8504. Treat it as unconfirmed scope. (3) The 2025 value (~$6.3B, 'CPA') has no URL. (4) Internal inconsistency (computed): $5.74B ÷ 20% implies a 2023 HS 8504 total of $28.7B. The same TrendEconomy page, as used in hts850423-2023 ($1.92B = 7.04%), implies a total of $27.27B. On that total, Mexico's share is about 21.0%, not 20%. This is a small gap, but both numbers supposedly come from the same page. (5) The primary source would be Census/USITC DataWeb by partner and HS 8504. It was not reached.

findings.claim: Mexico's own data show HS 8504 exports to the US of $7.08B in 2024, about 98% of Mexico's HS 8504 exports.
findings.detail: The next destinations are tiny: Canada $72.1M, Netherlands $57.3M, Hong Kong $24.7M, China $16.1M. The 98% is computed: 7.08 / (7.08 + 0.072 + 0.057 + 0.025 + 0.016) = 97.7%, a lower bound on the US share because smaller destinations are excluded. Mexico-reported exports ($7.08B) exceed US-reported imports ($6.18B, Trading Economics), which is a normal mirror gap.

findings.claim: Thailand ($3.3B) and Japan ($2.4B) were the third and fourth largest HS 8504 origins in 2025, after Mexico and China.
findings.detail: 2023 comparison (TrendEconomy): Thailand $2.11B (7.73%), Japan ~$1.36B (4.98%). These flows are mostly power supplies and converters, not utility transformers.

findings.claim: US HS 8504 imports from South Korea rose from about $1.29B in 2023 to $1.84B in 2024.
findings.detail: The 2023 figure is from TrendEconomy (4.7% share). The 2025 HS 8504 value from Korea was not found. Computed growth 2023 to 2024: +42.6%.

findings.claim: US HS 8504 imports from Vietnam were $1.66B in 2024 and rose about $1.4B over 2020-2025, while China's HS 8504 exports to Vietnam doubled from $1.5B to $3.0B.
findings.detail: The 2024 value is from Trading Economics (https://tradingeconomics.com/united-states/imports/vietnam/electrical-electronic-equipment). CPA calls this a transshipment signal, not confirmed evasion. It matters for EO 14420 enforcement, since Chinese-made content may arrive through ASEAN.

findings.claim: US HS 8504 imports from Canada were $1.51B in 2025, and Canada's 2024 exports of small liquid transformers (8504.21, ≤650 kVA) to the US were $130.7M for 15,568 units.
findings.detail: The 2025 total is from Trading Economics (https://tradingeconomics.com/united-states/imports/canada/electrical-electronic-equipment). Computed implied unit value for 8504.21 Canada→US 2024: $130,696k / 15,568 = ~$8,395 per unit, a distribution-class price proxy. Canada-reported HS 8504 exports to the US in 2024 were $1.60B.

findings.claim: US HS 8504 imports from India were about $1.29B in 2025.
findings.detail: Single-source table row (Trading Economics/Comtrade). McKinsey with IEEMA puts India's transformer exports at about $0.7B (all destinations) and India's share of global transformer exports at about 2.5% (https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/industrials/our-insights/wired-for-growth-indias-electrical-equipment-opportunity), so most of the $1.29B is likely converters and power supplies.

findings.claim: Brazil's 2025 HS 8504 exports to the US were about $660.7M.
findings.detail: Brazil matters mainly in large power: it was the #2 origin of >100 MVA units in 2025 (see lpt-100mva-origins-2025). Brazilian exports to the US overall fell 6.5% in Jan-Sep 2026 under US surcharges (Amcham via Band: https://www.band.com.br/economia/vendas-do-brasil-aos-eua-saltam-319-no-mes-mas-recuam-65-em-2026).

findings.claim: US imports under 8504.23 were about $1.92B in 2023, 7.04% of HS 8504.
findings.detail: This is the only 6-digit 8504.23 annual total found. DataMexico lists the US as the largest global 8504.23 importer at $1.02B, but its year label is ambiguous (likely 2022 BACI data), so it was not used.
findings.verify_evidence: No independent search was possible because the search budget was exhausted. The arithmetic implies a 2023 HS 8504 total of $1.92B / 0.0704 = $27.27B, which differs slightly from the $28.7B implied by the Mexico finding. TrendEconomy republishes UN Comtrade data, so it is S/W, not primary. USITC DataWeb or Census for HTS 8504.23.00 would be primary but was not reached. There is also a scope tension with lpt-100mva-2025. That finding has the >100 MVA slice alone at $2.77B in 2025. Since >100 MVA liquid units sit inside 8504.23 (>10 MVA), 8504.23 would have to grow well over 44% from 2023 to 2025 for both figures to be right. That is possible given the boom, but these two vendor-sourced numbers should be checked against each other in DataWeb before either is relied on.

findings.claim: US imports of liquid transformers above 100 MVA rose from 617 units ($0.62B) in 2019 to 2,268 units ($2.77B) in 2025.
findings.detail: Census-derived (via a vendor report). Computed implied unit value: 2019 $620M/617 = $1.005M; 2025 $2,770M/2,268 = $1.221M (+21.5%). Units grew 3.68x and value 4.47x. The ~$1.2M average looks low for >100 MVA units. Possible causes are disassembled shipments counted as several units, declared values below contract price, or the mix. Treat it as a customs-value proxy, not a transaction price. 2025 >100 MVA imports ($2.77B) exceed the whole of 8504.23 in 2023 ($1.92B), which fits rapid growth.
findings.verify_evidence: No independent search was possible because the search budget was exhausted. The arithmetic checks out (computed): $620M/617 = $1.005M per unit; $2,770M/2,268 = $1.221M; +21.5%; 3.68x units; 4.47x value. Plausibility problems: (a) The baseline PPI (indicators.csv) shows transformer prices up about 91% since Jan 2020, but the implied unit value rose only 21.5%. (b) A ~$1.2M average, and ~$0.71M for Mexico, is low for complete ≥100 MVA units. From memory, not re-checked this session, DOE's LPT report put LPT prices at roughly $2–7.5M in 2010 dollars. (c) Korea Customs values its whole >10 MVA export category to the US at $738M ÷ 323 units = $2.29M per unit. Read together, these suggest one of two things. Either the vendor's '>100 MVA' series counts components or partial shipments as units, or it actually covers a broader scope such as all of 8504.23 (>10 MVA). If it were all of 8504.23, the $2.77B in 2025 against $1.92B in 2023 would be ordinary growth rather than anomalous. Source quality: nextmsc (Next Move Strategy Consulting) is a vendor research page, so tag W/S, not P. Before using this, verify in Census/USITC DataWeb at the 10-digit statistical suffix for ≥100,000 kVA. I recall from DOE/BIS LPT work that this is 8504.23.0080, but I did not re-verify it.

findings.claim: Imports of >100 MVA liquid transformers reached 2,901 units in the 12 months to June 30, 2026.
findings.detail: Computed: 2,901 / 2,268 = +27.9% vs CY2025. Because the windows overlap, H1-2026 units exceeded H1-2025 units by 633. No TTM value was given. This is the most recent large-unit import datapoint found.
findings.verify_evidence: No independent search was possible because the search budget was exhausted. The arithmetic is correct (computed): 2,901/2,268 − 1 = +27.9%. Because TTM(Jun-26) = CY25 − H1-25 + H1-26, H1-2026 units exceed H1-2025 units by exactly 633. The figure inherits every scope and unit-count concern raised under lpt-100mva-2025. It comes from the same single vendor page and was not checked against Census monthly data for 2026 (DataWeb was not reached). The baseline says no clean 2026 HS 8504 import series is available, so this is a single-source, vendor-reported number.

findings.claim: Mexico (630 units), Brazil (343) and South Korea (323) supplied 57% of 2025 US imports of >100 MVA liquid transformers by units and 50% by value.
findings.detail: Computed unit shares from the 2,268 total: Mexico 27.8%, Brazil 15.1%, Korea 14.2%, together 57.1%. Computed top-3 value: 50% × $2.77B = ~$1.385B. The rest of the world is 972 units and ~$1.385B. Austria, Germany, Japan, Turkey and others make up the remainder, but their unit counts were not found. Compare the OSTI/DOE value shares in osti-lpt-origins.
findings.verify_evidence: No independent search was possible because the search budget was exhausted. The arithmetic is correct (computed): 630/2,268 = 27.8%, 343 = 15.1%, 323 = 14.2%, together 57.1%; remainder 972 units; 50% × $2.77B = $1.385B. A cross-check against Korea Customs data is only partly consistent. If Korea's 323 US-bound units carried its entire >10 MVA US export value ($738M), Brazil would be about $1,385M − $447M (Mexico) − $738M = ~$200M over 343 units, or ~$0.58M per unit (computed). That figure is also implausibly low for ≥100 MVA units, which again points to a unit-count or scope problem in the vendor series. The country ranking (Mexico, then Brazil and Korea) fits the baseline's view of Mexico as the largest source. The counts themselves are single-source vendor data.

findings.claim: Declared 2025 unit values for >100 MVA imports ranged from about $0.71M (Mexico) to about $2.43M (Austria).
findings.detail: Reported once and not reproduced on a second query, so tagged W. All figures below are computed from the inputs above. Mexico value ≈ 630 × $0.71M = $447M. Brazil+Korea combined value ≈ $1.385B − $0.447B = $0.938B over 666 units, a blended ~$1.41M per unit. Rest of world ≈ $1.385B/972 = ~$1.42M per unit. Korea cross-check upper bound: Korea Customs 2025 >10 MVA exports to the US of $738.28M ÷ 323 units = $2.29M per unit, which overstates because it includes 10-100 MVA units. Austria's premium likely reflects EHV and shell or large GSU mix, not like-for-like pricing.
findings.verify_evidence: No independent search was possible because the search budget was exhausted. The researcher already says this was reported once and not reproduced, so it is W. The derived numbers are computed correctly: 630 × $0.71M = $447.3M; ($1,385M − $447M)/666 = $1.41M; $1,385M/972 = $1.42M; $738.28M/323 = $2.29M. However, a $0.71M declared value for a ≥100 MVA liquid-filled unit is far below normal LPT pricing. That makes the Mexico figure more likely evidence of a unit-count or scope problem, such as partial shipments, or 10–100 MVA units included, than evidence of cheap Mexican LPTs. Do not use it as a price benchmark for a manufacturing business case.

findings.claim: China supplied only about 2.2% of US >100 MVA liquid transformer units in 2025, even though WoodMac counts more than 8,000 'high-power' Chinese units imported through Oct 2025.
findings.detail: Computed: ~0.022 × 2,268 ≈ 50 units. The two figures fit together if the >8,000 Chinese units (WoodMac via CPA and Bloomberg/Yahoo) are mostly 10-100 MVA substation and data-center units and smaller. WoodMac's Boucher told CNBC China's share is near 30% only in 'certain' transformer and switchgear categories (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/03/us-ai-data-centers-china-supply-chain.html). Goldman puts China at about 4% of the US transformer market. I trust the Census-based >100 MVA share for LPTs and read the 30% as a mid-size and smaller category figure. EO 14420 exposure therefore sits mostly below 100 MVA.
findings.verify_evidence: No independent search was possible because the search budget was exhausted, so the CNBC Boucher quote, the Goldman '~4%' figure (no URL given) and the 2.2% figure were not checked. Computed: 0.022 × 2,268 ≈ 50 units. Both the baseline (market-map section 6) and this finding cite '>8,000 high-power Chinese units through Oct 2025'. There is also a contradiction with the baseline worth stating explicitly. The baseline (indicators.csv; weekly/2026-10-11.md) cites WoodMac saying more than $22B of bulk-power imports are exposed to EO 14420 and that 'the 100 MVA+ segment [is] hit hardest'. This finding concludes exposure 'sits mostly below 100 MVA'. Both can be true only if WoodMac's 'hit hardest' describes the resulting shortage or deficit, not China's share of imports. Also, $22B is about 8x the total $2.77B of >100 MVA imports, so most of that exposure must lie in inverters, BESS, breakers and smaller transformers. The reconciliation is reasonable but rests on one vendor series with doubtful unit counts.

findings.claim: A DOE-sponsored OSTI report lists Mexico (19%), Brazil (12%) and South Korea (9%) as top origins of finished >100 MVA transformers, with about 80% import reliance.
findings.detail: The extracted text is garbled, so the year and basis are uncertain. The report's import series covers 2015-2024 and says LPT imports were flat through 2021 and jumped in 2022. The ranking matches the NextMSC 2025 unit data: Mexico, then Brazil, then Korea.

findings.claim: Korea Customs data show Korea's >10 MVA transformer exports to the US at $257.97M (2023), $403.45M (2024) and a record $738.28M (2025).
findings.detail: Korean customs statistics via Asia Business Daily and Kmib (https://www.kmib.co.kr/article/view.asp?arcid=1768811387). Interim cumulative 2025 totals: Jan-Oct $630.38M and Jan-Nov $690.93M (+115.6% YoY). Computed growth: 2024 +56.4%, 2025 +83.0%. Computed 2025 monthly average: $61.5M.
findings.verify_evidence: No independent search was possible because the search budget was exhausted, so the 2023 ($257.97M) and 2024 ($403.45M) values were not checked. Partial corroboration: the 2025 US figure of about $738M matches a separate source already in the baseline (indicators.csv line 18; transformer-magazine.com: record $1.3B total Korean UHV exports, ~$738M to the US). I did not re-open that page this session. The arithmetic is correct (computed): 2024 +56.4%, 2025 +83.0%, monthly average $61.52M; implied Nov-2025 $60.55M and Dec-2025 $47.35M. One soft inconsistency (computed): if Jan–Nov 2025 ($690.93M) is +115.6% YoY, Jan–Nov 2024 was about $320.5M. That leaves about $83M for Dec-2024 alone (out of $403.45M full-year), which is high relative to other months. Check whether the +115.6% applies to Jan–Nov or to a different window. Scope note: the Korean customs 'UHV' category is >10 MVA, the same as US 8504.23, not >100 MVA.

findings.claim: Korea shipped $595.58M of ultra-high-voltage transformers to the US in January-July 2026, per KITA data reported by Herald.
findings.detail: Computed: $85.1M per month vs $61.5M per month in 2025 (+38%). The annualized run-rate is ~$1.02B, consistent with the Korean press forecast of >KRW1.5T for 2026. The same article gives US tonnage as 2,639 tons, which would imply ~$225,700/ton, about 10x Korea's reported $/ton. The tonnage is likely misreported, so only the dollar value is used. No Jan-Jul 2025 comparison was found.

findings.claim: The US took about 72% of Korea's ultra-high-voltage transformer exports in Jan-Jul 2026, up from about 57% in 2025 and 43% in 2024.
findings.detail: Computed: $595.58M US ÷ $822.32M global (Jan-Jul 2026) = 72.4%. For 2025: $738.28M ÷ ~$1.3B (KITA global >10 MVA) = ~57%. The 2022, 2023 and 2024 shares of 28%, 38% and 43% (>10 MVA) and the 63.3% US share of all Korean transformer exports in 2024 (KITA) come from https://view.asiae.co.kr/en/article/2025112115304499997. Korean capacity is being redirected to the US.

findings.claim: Korea's US-bound ultra-high-voltage transformer export price rose to $22,920 per ton in 2025 from $19,060 in 2024 (+20.2%), 17.5% above Korea's world average of $19,495 per ton.
findings.detail: Herald Economy citing KITA. The article prints US tonnage as '3,320만톤', a unit error. Computed: $738.28M ÷ $22,920 = ~32,210 tons. This is the cleanest large-unit price proxy found: imported EHV prices rose ~20% in one year, and tariffs were passed through.

findings.claim: Korea's global ultra-high-voltage transformer exports set an H1 record of $701.52M in 2026 and reached $822.32M (39,747 tons) in Jan-Jul 2026.
findings.detail: The H1 figure is Korean customs data via Businesskorea. Jan-Jul is from Herald (https://biz.heraldcorp.com/article/10845591). Computed: H1-2026 vs H1-2025 ($664.2M per Herald, https://biz.heraldcorp.com/article/10536090, year inferred from consistency with the 2025 total) = +5.6%, so global growth is slow while US-bound growth is strong. Computed Jan-Jul unit price: $822.32M ÷ 39,747 t = $20,689/t. The article states $26,890/t (+6.2%), which does not reconcile, so the computed figure is preferred.

findings.claim: Korea's pole-mount transformer exports (oil-immersed, ≤100 kV) averaged only about $18M in Q2 2025, down more than half year on year, as small Korean makers lost US orders.
findings.detail: KOEMA data via Electimes. Cited causes: more US supply sources, tariff risk, and quality problems (overweight units, design defects) that sent buyers to Latin American suppliers. This is the opposite of the EHV trend: imported distribution supply is contestable.

findings.claim: KIET ranks Korea first in the US import market for high-voltage power cables and second for extra-high-voltage transformers.
findings.detail: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade research report. The year of ranking data was not given in the snippet.

findings.claim: China's 2025 transformer exports were a record RMB64.6B (+~36%), and the average export price per unit rose about one-third to RMB205,000.
findings.detail: People's Daily citing GACC. The unit-price datapoint is new to the baseline. Goldman (via press) says >10 MVA exports grew 52% in 2025.

findings.claim: China's transformer exports totaled $7.95B in Jan-Aug 2026 (+28.5%), with August at $1.067B (+14.8%), the slowest growth this year.
findings.detail: Caixin Securities note citing GACC. The note names the US as the single largest demand country and attributes the slowdown to large-capacity units and EU/Asia/Africa markets. A separate RMB series (Jiemian, https://www.jiemian.com/article/14975642.html) gives Jan-Jul RMB42.63B (+26.0%) and July RMB6.95B (+22.3%). ksher's H1 RMB39.79B (+26.78%) conflicts with that series (it would imply July = RMB2.84B), so the brokerage/Jiemian figures are preferred.

findings.claim: China's liquid-dielectric transformer exports fell 2.6% YoY to RMB4.21B in August 2026, and North America-bound shipments, though +111% YoY, dropped 35.7% from July.
findings.detail: Changjiang Securities. Jan-Aug liquid-transformer total: RMB33.294B (+25.07%). By size in August: 400-500 MVA +406.6% YoY, >500 MVA −78.5% YoY. EO 14420 was signed Aug 26, so August mostly predates it. September GACC data (due ~Oct 18-20) will be the first clean post-EO month.

findings.claim: China's US-bound transformer export growth slowed from +182% (Jan-Feb 2026, >10 MVA) to +118% (Mar) and +95% (Apr), and was about +45% for all transformers in H1 2026, with the US the #1 destination at 11%.
findings.detail: The monthly figures come from the Goldman Sachs note of Mar 26, 2026 via Sina. In Jan-Feb, >10 MVA exports were RMB4.4B (+61%), and US-bound units were mostly 10-220 MVA. The H1 +45% and 11% share are single-source (ksher, https://www.ksher.cn/news/post/wmb2b26090406/, W). The baseline had only the Jan-Feb +182%.

findings.claim: China's transformer export value rose 31.3% in Jan-May 2026 while the average unit price rose 22.3%.
findings.detail: Brokerage summary citing GACC. Computed volume effect: (1.313/1.223) − 1 ≈ +7.4% units, so most of China's export growth is price and mix, not volume.

findings.claim: Census shows imports in the 'Generators, accessories' end-use line at $33.38B for Jan-Aug 2026 vs $32.62B a year earlier (+2.3%), with August at $4.38B vs $4.16B in July.
findings.detail: Column headers were not visible in the extract. I read them as Aug, Jul, change, then YTD 2026, YTD 2025, change, per the FT-900 Exhibit 7 layout. Computed: 758/32,618 = +2.3%. Trading Economics labels this Census series 'Generators, Transformers & Accessories'. It mixes gensets and transformers, so treat it as a broad indicator that 2026 electrical-equipment import growth has flattened.

result.analysis:
Five conclusions for someone planning to build transformers in the US.

1. Imported large-power demand is still growing fast. US imports of liquid transformers above 100 MVA rose from 617 units in 2019 to 2,268 units ($2.77B) in 2025, and to 2,901 units in the 12 months to June 2026, about 28% above 2025 (lpt-100mva-2025, lpt-100mva-ttm-2026). The domestic capacity due in 2027-29 will arrive in a short market, not a saturated one.

2. The competitors are allies and near-shore suppliers, not China. Mexico, Brazil and Korea supplied 57% of >100 MVA units in 2025. China supplied about 2% (lpt-100mva-origins-2025, china-lpt-share). The DOE-sponsored OSTI report ranks the same three origins first (osti-lpt-origins). EO 14420 therefore mainly hits the 10-220 MVA data-center flow from China, not the large-power core. That flow was already slowing: China's US-bound growth fell from +182% in Jan-Feb to about +45% for H1, and North America-bound liquid shipments dropped 36% month on month in August (china-us-2026-path, china-liquid-aug-na).
   - Mexico is the low-price competitor, with declared values around $0.71M per unit (lpt-unit-values-country, W-grade).
   - Korea has pricing power: US-bound $/ton rose 20% in 2025 (korea-unit-price). Korea's US shipments run at about $1.0B a year in 2026, and about 72% of Korean ultra-high-voltage exports now go to the US (korea-us-uhv-2026-janjul, korea-us-share-of-exports).

3. Prices are high, but growth is slowing in places. China's export unit prices rose 22% in Jan-May 2026 (china-unit-price-2026), and Korean prices rose about 20%. Against that:
   - Korea's global ultra-high-voltage exports grew only about 6% in H1 2026 (korea-global-uhv-2026).
   - China's August growth fell to 15% (china-2026-janaug).
   - Census's broad generators line is up only 2.3% year to date (census-enduse-generators).
   Exporters are moving existing capacity to the US rather than adding a lot of new supply. That supports current pricing but is not proof of a permanent shortage.

4. Trade protection is uneven by segment. In the large-power segment:
   - Extra-high-voltage units carry only a 15% Section 232 rate through 2027 (sec232-transformer-tiers).
   - The antidumping order on Korea is 0% for HD Hyundai and Iljin and 4.32% for LS Electric and Hyosung (korea-ad-final-2026).
   So a new US large-power plant gets little tariff shelter against the strongest imports. Distribution transformers carry 25%, and small Korean distribution exporters have retreated (korea-pole-transformers). That makes distribution, pad-mount and 10-100 MVA units the segments where tariffs plus freight and lead time favor a US plant. US-designed, India-built suppliers (Ayr Energy, Zetwerk) are moving into the same space and are already in a Section 337 case against each other (india-asset-light-importers, section337-ayr-zetwerk).

5. Several baseline items change. The baseline's "Mexico ~$2.3B in 2023, ~20% of HS 8504" mixes two scopes: Mexico's HS 8504 total was $5.74B in 2023, $6.18B in 2024 and about $6.3B in 2025 (mexico-8504-contradiction, mexico-datamexico-2024). The baseline's China datapoints should also be read by size class (china-lpt-share).

The main remaining gap is HS-10 monthly country data for 2026, especially for 10-100 MVA units and the September post-EO month. It can be pulled from the Census API.

findings.claim: The BLS PPI for power and distribution transformers ex parts (WPU117409) printed a record 381.783 in Jul 2026, +8.7% YoY and +4.6% MoM.
findings.detail: Computed: 381.783/351.192 (Jul 2025, ALFRED vintage) = +8.71%; 381.783/364.861 (Jun 2026) = +4.64%. The prior record was 351.192 (Jul-Sep 2025). July is preliminary until BLS revises it four months later. 381.783/199.5 (Jan 2020 per NextMSC/LaborDataHub, not verified on FRED) = +91.4%.
findings.correction: 381.783 (Jul 2026), +8.7% YoY and +4.6% MoM, all confirmed. One detail is wrong: the previous high was 365.135 (Oct-Dec 2025) or 366.604 (Jan 2026 first print), not 351.192 (Jul-Sep 2025).
findings.verify_evidence: FRED WPU117409 (updated Aug 13, 2026; next release Oct 15, 2026) shows Jul 2026 = 381.783, Jun/May/Apr 2026 = 364.861 and Mar 2026 = 362.638. Trading Economics (data through Sep 2025, updated Dec 2025) shows Sep 2025 = 351.192 and names Jul 2025 = 351.192 as the record at that time. Computed: 381.783/351.192 = +8.71% and 381.783/364.861 = +4.64%. Both match. The 'record' label holds. However, the finding's detail says the prior record was 351.192, and that is wrong. A FRED WPU11740999 snapshot (the vintage that carried Jan 2026 = 366.604) lists Oct, Nov and Dec 2025 each at 365.135. So the series passed 351.192 in Oct 2025, and Jul 2026 beats a high of about 365-367, not 351. The Jan 2020 base of 199.5 (+91.4%) appears only in NextMSC's table. I could not confirm it on FRED; it is consistent with NextMSC's own +80.6% for 2019-2025. Flag: the WPU117409 FRED page still showed 'Updated Aug 13, 2026' when the parent WPU1174 had been updated Sep 10 with August data. An August 2026 print for this commodity either was not published or was not captured. Check BLS on Oct 15.
findings.corrected_value: 381.783 (Jul 2026), +8.7% YoY and +4.6% MoM, all confirmed. One detail is wrong: the previous high was 365.135 (Oct-Dec 2025) or 366.604 (Jan 2026 first print), not 351.192 (Jul-Sep 2025).

findings.claim: After the Sep 10, 2026 PPI release, FRED's WPU117409 page still showed Jul 2026 as its latest observation (updated Aug 13, next release Oct 15), so no Aug 2026 value appears to have been published for this series.
findings.detail: Inference: sibling series WPU1174, PCU335311335311 and PCU335311335311P were all updated Sep 10, 2026 with Aug values, but the WPU117409 page was not. Possible causes are a BLS publication withhold for August (insufficient reports) or a FRED lag. Verify on data.bls.gov. For Aug 2026 tracking, use WPU1174 or PCU335311335311. Sep data is due Oct 15, 2026.

findings.claim: Later FRED vintages put WPU117409/WPU11740999 at 362.638 for Jan-Mar 2026 and 364.861 for Apr-Jun 2026. This supersedes the baseline's 366.604 for Jan 2026 and the 365.306 first print for Apr-May.
findings.detail: FRED carries this BLS commodity under two IDs with identical titles and matching overlapping values (Mar 2026 = 362.638 on both). The Jun 11, 2026 vintage of WPU11740999 shows Jan-Mar 362.638 and Apr-May 365.306. The Aug 13, 2026 vintage of WPU117409 shows Mar 362.638 and Apr-Jun 364.861. The baseline's 366.604 for Jan 2026 was most likely a first print later revised down about 1.1%. I trust the later vintage.
findings.verify_evidence: The two vintages match the finding. The FRED WPU11740999 snapshot updated Jun 11, 2026 shows Jan, Feb and Mar 2026 = 362.638 and Apr and May 2026 = 365.306. The FRED/ALFRED WPU117409 snapshot updated Aug 13, 2026 shows Mar 2026 = 362.638, Apr-Jun 2026 = 364.861 and Jul 2026 = 381.783. An earlier WPU11740999 snapshot shows Jan 2026 = 366.604 (the baseline's figure) and Oct-Dec 2025 = 365.135. Computed revision: 362.638/366.604 = -1.08%, which matches the finding's 'about 1.1%'. Jan 2026 was first published in late Feb 2026 and revised in the June vintage, which fits BLS's practice of revising four months after first publication (that schedule is my background knowledge, not a fetched source). Two caveats. (1) The Apr-May change from 365.306 to 364.861 shows up in the Aug 13 vintage, earlier than that normal schedule would revise April. (2) Searches could not confirm that WPU117409 and WPU11740999 are literally the same BLS series rather than a re-coded successor; they share a title and base and have equal Mar 2026 values. Baseline update: indicators.csv row '2026-01, WPU11740999, 366.604' is a superseded first print.

findings.claim: WPU117409 moved in discrete steps: flat at 351.192 in Jul-Sep 2025, 362.638 in Jan-Mar 2026 (+3.3%), 364.861 in Apr-Jun (+0.6%), then 381.783 in Jul 2026 (+4.6%).
findings.detail: Computed from FRED and ALFRED vintages: 362.638/351.192 = +3.26%; 364.861/362.638 = +0.61%; 381.783/364.861 = +4.64%. Oct-Dec 2025 values were not retrieved. Implication: realized transformer prices reset in periodic list or contract steps (around the turn of the year and mid-year) rather than drifting monthly.
findings.verify_evidence: The finding left out Oct-Dec 2025, and those months change the picture. A FRED WPU11740999 snapshot lists Oct 2025 = Nov 2025 = Dec 2025 = 365.135, followed by Jan 2026 = 366.604 (first print). So the first step up from 351.192 came in October 2025, not at the turn of the year. Computed: 365.135/351.192 = +3.97%. The revised Jan-Mar 2026 level of 362.638 is slightly below Oct-Dec 2025 (computed -0.68%), unless those 2025 months were also revised later; I could not see a later vintage for them. Trading Economics confirms Sep 2025 = 351.192 with Jul 2025 = 351.192 as the high at the time, which supports the flat Jul-Sep run. The broad point still holds: the series moves in discrete steps rather than monthly drift, here in October and July. But the 'around the turn of the year' timing is wrong. Context: BLS cancelled the standalone October 2025 PPI release because of the Oct 1-Nov 12, 2025 funding lapse and collected October data late, publishing it with November on Jan 14, 2026, so the October step was a late-collected observation.

findings.claim: The NAICS 335311 industry PPI (PCU335311335311) hit a record 475.065 in Aug 2026, +7.8% YoY (Aug 2025: 440.550) and +0.05% MoM.
findings.detail: Jul 2026 474.831 (+3.99% MoM from Jun 456.602); Aug 475.065. Aug 2025 = 440.550 per the Nov 25, 2025 FRED vintage. Computed YoY: 475.065/440.550 = +7.83%. The baseline's latest reading was Mar 2026 at 455.9 (+4.27% YoY), so YoY growth nearly doubled between March and August.
findings.verify_evidence: FRED PCU335311335311 (updated Sep 10, 2026; next release Oct 15) shows Aug 2026 = 475.065, Jul 2026 = 474.831, Jun and May 2026 = 456.602 and Apr 2026 = 454.338. Computed: Jul MoM 474.831/456.602 = +3.99%; Aug MoM 475.065/474.831 = +0.05%. The 'record' label holds: 475.065 is above both Oct 2025 = 458.356 (FRED and Trading Economics) and Dec 2025-Feb 2026 = 458.462 (FRED, Mar 18, 2026 vintage). The Aug 2025 base of 440.550 is only weakly corroborated. LaborDataHub's page for this NAICS series shows an undated 'Index Value: 440.550', and I could not find it on FRED or ALFRED in search. It is plausible: LaborDataHub's Mar 2026 = 455.9 at +4.27% YoY implies Mar 2025 of about 437.2 (computed). So the +7.83% YoY rests on a base I could not independently pin to August 2025. The baseline's Mar 2026 455.9 (+4.27%) is confirmed by LaborDataHub. July and August 2026 values are preliminary until BLS revises them.

findings.claim: PCU335311335311 peaked at 458.356 in Oct 2025, slipped to 454.338 by Apr 2026 (-0.9%), and held at about 456.6 in May-Jun 2026 before the July jump.
findings.detail: The Oct 2025 record is per Trading Economics (FRED data, Jul 2026 update). TE showed May 2026 at 457.057; the later FRED vintage has 456.602, a small revision. Apr-Jun values come from FRED's Sep 10, 2026 vintage. Computed: 454.338/458.356 = -0.88%. WPU1174 shows the same pattern (Feb 2026 421.523 to Apr 415.235, -1.5%). The Q4'25-Q2'26 deceleration was real, but it ended in July.
findings.correction: A plateau of about 458.4 from Oct 2025 through Feb 2026 (Oct 458.356; Dec 2025, Jan 2026 and Feb 2026 = 458.462 in the Mar 18, 2026 FRED vintage), then 454.338 in Apr 2026 (-0.9%) and 456.602 in May-Jun 2026
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmed: Oct 2025 = 458.356 (FRED snippet, and Trading Economics, which names it the record high in its Jul 2026 update); Apr 2026 = 454.338 and May/Jun 2026 = 456.602 (FRED, Sep 10, 2026); Trading Economics May 2026 = 457.057, a small revision. The single peak in October is not secure, though. A FRED PCU335311335311 snapshot updated Mar 18, 2026 lists Dec 2025 = Jan 2026 = Feb 2026 = 458.462, slightly above 458.356. Trading Economics' July 2026 record label implies those months were later revised below 458.356, but I could not see the revised values. So it is safer to describe a flat top of about 458.4 running Oct 2025-Feb 2026. The size of the dip is the same either way: 454.338/458.356 = -0.88% and 454.338/458.462 = -0.90%. The WPU1174 comparison holds: Trading Economics gives Feb 2026 = 421.523 as a record and FRED gives Apr 2026 = 415.235, a computed -1.49%. That also shows the commodity index peaked in Feb 2026, not Oct 2025. Related: the Primary Products series (P) hit a record 451.856 in Dec 2025 (Trading Economics) and was at 449.476 in Jun 2026, so the soft patch shows up there too.
findings.corrected_value: A plateau of about 458.4 from Oct 2025 through Feb 2026 (Oct 458.356; Dec 2025, Jan 2026 and Feb 2026 = 458.462 in the Mar 18, 2026 FRED vintage), then 454.338 in Apr 2026 (-0.9%) and 456.602 in May-Jun 2026

findings.claim: The PPI for NAICS 335311 primary products (PCU335311335311P) was 467.897 in Aug 2026, +7.6% YoY, up from +3.8% YoY in Jun 2026.
The PPI for transformers and power regulators (WPU1174) was a record 434.493 in Aug 2026, +7.6% YoY, after dipping from 421.523 (Feb 2026) to 415.235 (Apr 2026).
findings.verify_evidence: FRED WPU1174 (updated Sep 10, 2026) shows Aug 2026 = 434.493, Jul 2026 = 434.315, Jun and May 2026 = 416.959 and Apr 2026 = 415.235. An older FRED snapshot (Sep 2025) shows Apr-Jun 2025 = 402.300 and Jul-Aug 2025 = 403.758. Trading Economics (updated Mar 2026) gives Feb 2026 = 421.523, a record high at the time, so Aug 2026 at 434.493 is a new record. Recomputed: 434.493/403.758 = +7.61%; 416.959/402.300 = +3.64%; 434.315/416.959 = +4.16%; 434.493/434.315 = +0.04%. All match. Caveat: the 2025 bases come from the Sep 2025 vintage, when Jul and Aug 2025 were still preliminary, so final 2025 values could differ slightly. The repeated May/Jun 2026 value may be carried forward rather than an actual unchanged price.

findings.claim: Across all four transformer PPIs, YoY growth roughly doubled, from 3.6-4.1% in Jun 2026 to 7.6-8.7% in Jul-Aug 2026. Price growth is reaccelerating, not decelerating as the baseline states.
findings.detail: Computed (see momentum table). Jun 2026 YoY: WPU117409 +4.1%, PCU335311335311 +4.0%, P series +3.8%, WPU1174 +3.6%. Jul/Aug YoY: +8.7%, +7.8%, +7.6%, +7.6%. The whole change comes from one July step (+4.0 to +4.6% MoM); August was flat (+0.04 to +0.05%). In real terms, BLS PPI final demand rose +4.7% YoY in July and +5.4% in August (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ppi.htm), so transformer prices are outrunning general producer inflation by about 2-4 points.
findings.verify_evidence: Independently checked inputs. Primary Products series (P): YCharts Jun 2025 = 433.13 and Jul/Aug 2025 = 434.73; FRED Jun 2026 = 449.476, Jul 2026 = 467.689, Aug 2026 = 467.897. Computed: Jun YoY +3.77%, Jul +7.58%, Aug +7.63%, Aug MoM +0.04%. WPU1174: +3.64% to +7.61% (FRED). WPU117409 Jul: +8.71%. BLS final demand: +4.7% for the 12 months ended July 2026 (BLS TED, original July figure; the August release revised July's monthly change) and +5.4% for the 12 months ended August 2026 (BLS TED; release dated Sep 10, 2026). So the 'outrunning by about 2-4 points' claim holds (computed 7.6-8.7 minus 4.7-5.4). Not independently verified: the Jun 2025 base for WPU117409 (needed for +4.1%) and the Jun and Aug 2025 bases for PCU335311335311 (+4.0% and +7.8%); 440.550 has only an undated LaborDataHub mention. Caveats: July-August 2026 are preliminary prints; WPU117409 shows no August 2026 value yet; and the whole re-acceleration comes from one July step. This contradicts the baseline's 'decelerating' label, which rested on Mar 2026 data.

findings.claim: A Mississippi PSC filing in MISO's cost-estimation-guide proceeding reports WPU117409 changes of +3.0% (2019), +2.6% (2020), +33.4% (2021) and +20.7% (2022).
findings.detail: The MPSC used the PPI as a proxy for transformer materials and fabrication costs and urged MISO to revisit its cost data rather than apply a single adjustment factor. The measurement basis (annual average vs Dec/Dec) is not stated in the excerpt. The timing differs from the industry series (Dec/Dec +17.3% in 2021 and +34.6% in 2022), but both show a 2021-22 surge of about 60% cumulatively.

findings.claim: The discontinued BLS industry product index for power and distribution transformers (PCU3353113353111) was 197.30 in Dec 2019, 200.00 in Dec 2020, 234.58 in Dec 2021, 315.71 in Dec 2022 and 333.1 in Feb 2023 (+20.5% YoY), and then ended.
findings.detail: December values are from YCharts. The Feb 2023 value of 333.1, record 336.3 and YoY +20.52% are from GuruFocus (https://www.gurufocus.com/economic_indicators/3789/...). FRED data for this series runs Dec 1999 to Feb 2023. Computed Dec/Dec changes: 2020 +1.4%, 2021 +17.3%, 2022 +34.6%.

findings.claim: A secondary analysis of WPU117409 puts annual-average growth at +34.6% (2022), +6.7% (2023), +2.7% (2024) and +3.0% (2025), with a 2026 YTD average of 366.3 (+5.0%).
findings.detail: This conflicts with a vendor claim (via distroforge/electricaltrader) of 20-25% growth in 2023 and 15% in 2024. I trust the NextMSC numbers more because they match the level check in ppi-plateau-check and Trading Economics' Jul 2025 record of 351.192. Verify against a FRED CSV.
findings.verify_evidence: NextMSC's page (dated Oct 5, 2026) does report these figures. Annual-average transformer PPI: 2022 = 312.6 (+34.6%), 2023 = 333.4 (+6.7%), 2024 = 342.5 (+2.7%), 2025 = 352.9 (+3.0%), 2026 YTD = 366.3 (+5.0%). NextMSC says it computed these from BLS monthly data via FRED. Definition matters: the +5.0% compares Jan-Jul 2026 with Jan-Jul 2025. It is not 2026 YTD against the 2025 full-year average, which would be 366.3/352.9 = +3.8% (computed). Internal checks I ran: 342.5/333.4 = +2.7%; 352.9/342.5 = +3.0%; 333.4/312.6 = +6.7%. Recomputing the Jan-Jul 2026 average from revised FRED values (3 x 362.638, 3 x 364.861, 1 x 381.783) gives 366.33, which matches 366.3. The 2025 average of 352.9 is consistent with Jul-Sep 351.192 and Oct-Dec 365.135 if Jan-Jun 2025 averaged about 347.6 (implied, not observed). I could not get a FRED annual CSV through search, so the annual averages remain NextMSC's own calculations. A level of about 312-333 in 2022-23 is consistent with GuruFocus's related industry series PCU3353113353111 (Feb 2023 = 333.1). The vendor claim of 20-25% in 2023 and 15% in 2024 was not found in any primary source and is inconsistent with the PPI. Note that NextMSC rebases its charts to Jan 2020 = 100, so its % figures are best read as computed off FRED levels.

findings.claim: An independent level check supports a 2023 to mid-2025 plateau: the BLS power and distribution transformer index was 333.1 in Feb 2023, and WPU117409 was 351.192 in Jul 2025, roughly +5% over 2.5 years.
findings.detail: Computed: 351.192/333.1 = +5.4%. Caution: this compares the industry series PCU3353113353111 with the commodity series WPU117409. They share the same Dec 1999 base but are different series, so the comparison is indicative only. YCharts' P-series Dec 2023 (420.12) to Dec 2024 (426.83) gives +1.6%, which agrees, though YCharts flags inconsistencies on that page.

findings.claim: The PPI for other transformers and transformer parts (WPU117411) fell from 247.039 (Jan-Mar 2026) to 234.725 in Apr 2026 (-5.0%) and then rose to 240.545 in May 2026.
findings.detail: Values are from the Jun 11, 2026 FRED vintage. Later months were not retrieved. Specialty and other transformers and parts are much softer than power and distribution units.

findings.claim: The switchgear and switchboard apparatus PPI (PCU335313335313) reached 411.453 in Aug 2026, +13.1% YoY and +3.6% MoM, outpacing transformers.
findings.detail: 2026: Apr 394.279, May 394.814, Jun 394.815, Jul 397.292, Aug 411.453. Aug 2025 = 363.688 (Sep 2025 vintage). Computed: 411.453/363.688 = +13.13%; Aug MoM +3.56%. NextMSC (weak source) reports switchgear +89.4% vs Jan 2020. Relevant if an entrant sells packaged substations.

findings.claim: The broader NAICS 335 PPI rose to 221.071 in Aug 2026 (+0.5% MoM), while the PPI for electronic coils, transformers and inductors stayed near 199-203.
findings.detail: NAICS 335: May 217.160 (revised), Jun 218.068, Jul 219.927, Aug 221.071. Electronic coils/transformers commodity index WPU11785399: Jan 2026 196.997, May 2026 198.538 (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/WPU11785399). Industry index PCU33441K33441K6: Jun 2026 203.020. Small electronic transformers are not seeing grid-transformer inflation.

findings.claim: BLS's HS 8504 import price index for electrical transformers (IP8504) last shows Dec 2021 (119.9), so no current transformer-specific import price index is available.
findings.detail: The FRED page was last updated Jan 14, 2022 yet still lists future release dates; treat it as frozen or discontinued. The best available proxy is the broad NAICS 335 import index (mxp-iz335-flat). For transformer-specific landed prices, use Census trade unit values for HS 8504.21-8504.34.

findings.claim: The BLS import price index for NAICS 335 electrical equipment was 126.9 in Aug 2026 vs 127.0 in Aug 2025 (-0.1% YoY). BLS's Jun 2026 table showed -1.1% over 12 months.
findings.detail: Monthly values: Jun 2025 126.9r, Jul 2025 126.6r, Aug 2025 127.0, Sep 2025 125.8; Jul 2026 126.7 (+0.6% MoM), Aug 2026 126.9 (+0.2%). FRED IZ335 shows Feb-Mar 2026 126.8, Apr 125.3, May 125.4, Jun 125.5 (first prints; BLS revised May to 125.7 and Jun to 126.0). Computed YoY: 126.9/127.0 = -0.08%. All US import prices rose +7.0% YoY in Aug 2026 (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ximpim.nr0.htm). Caveat: NAICS 335 is broad (appliances, lighting, wiring devices), not transformers only.

findings.claim: BLS import price indexes are mostly quoted FOB foreign port and exclude duties. The flat NAICS 335 import index alongside about 8% domestic transformer PPI growth therefore reflects pre-tariff prices and understates landed-cost inflation.
findings.detail: BLS explains that duties are excluded to match BEA's GDP net-exports deflation. Implication: foreign sellers are not raising pre-duty prices, while domestic producer prices are rising. The domestic-vs-import gap is the tariff wedge (50% on electrical steel articles, 25% on copper-intensive derivatives per the baseline) plus scarcity. This supports domestic production economics but depends on policy.

findings.claim: LME copper (World Bank Pink Sheet) averaged $14,326/t in Aug 2026 and $14,474/t in Sep 2026, vs $9,670 and $9,984 a year earlier: +48.1% and +45.0% YoY.
findings.detail: The 2025 values come from the Sep 2025 and Oct 2025 Pink Sheets (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/18675f1d1639c7a34d463f59263ba0a2-0050012025/related/CMO-Pink-Sheet-October-2025.pdf): Jun 9,835, Jul 9,771, Aug 9,670, Sep 9,984. Column alignment was inferred by the search tool. It is corroborated by the World Bank blog (copper -1.0% in Aug 2025) and by Jul 2026 13,543 matching the IMF series exactly. Computed: Jul 2026 YoY +38.6%, Aug +48.1%, Sep +45.0%. Q3 2026 average is about 14,114.

findings.claim: The IMF global copper price (via FRED) rose from $12,529/t in Mar 2026 to $13,552/t in Jun 2026 and $13,543/t in Jul 2026, vs a 2025 annual average of $9,946.88/t.
COMEX copper monthly averages rose from $5.02/lb (Oct 2025) to $6.588/lb (Aug 2026), with Sep 2026 at about $6.58/lb.
findings.detail: CN Wire table: Oct 2025 5.0198, Nov 5.0196, Dec 5.3988, Jan 2026 5.8810, Feb 5.8590, Mar 5.6517, Apr 5.9036, May 6.2642, Jun 6.3223 (a duplicate entry shows 6.3224), Jul 6.2802, Aug 6.5880. International Wire gives Sep 2026 as 6.5809. Sources conflict on the all-time intraday record ($6.83 on Sep 22, $6.87 in early Aug, and the baseline's $6.89 on Sep 9); treat it as unverified. USGS MCS 2026 projected a record 2025 COMEX average of $4.80/lb.

findings.claim: The COMEX premium over LME has shrunk to about 1.4% (Aug 2026) and about 0.2% (Sep 2026), from about $1/lb before refined cathode was exempted from tariffs at end-Jul 2025.
findings.detail: Computed: LME Aug 14,326/2,204.62 = $6.498/lb vs COMEX 6.588 = +1.4%; LME Sep 14,474/2,204.62 = $6.565/lb vs COMEX 6.581 = +0.2%. Recycling Today reported the spread near $1/lb before the Jul 31, 2025 announcement and 6 cents/lb by mid-Aug 2025. US mills' copper cost now tracks LME closely until the refined-copper tariff phases in (15% in 2027 per the baseline). Hedging on LME or COMEX is roughly equivalent for now.

findings.claim: The PPI for copper wire and cable (WPU10260314) reached 602.480 in Aug 2026: +4.2% MoM, +12.9% since Apr 2026, and about +19% YoY in July.
findings.detail: 2026: Apr 533.808, May 564.877, Jun 577.166, Jul 578.187, Aug 602.480. Jul 2025 = 486.209 (record at the time, per Trading Economics). Computed: Jul YoY 578.187/486.209 = +18.9%. The Copper and Copper Products special index (WPUSI019011) was 799.699 in Aug 2026, above the May 2026 record of 777.462 per TE. Copper and brass mill shapes (WPU102502) were 785.472 in Jul 2026. The task named PCU331422331422; that exact ID did not surface, and WPU10260314 is the closest commodity series.

findings.claim: The cold-rolled steel sheet and strip PPI (WPU101707) reached 469.251 in Aug 2026, +27.6% since Nov 2025 (367.621), but still 34% below its Nov 2021 record of 711.611.
findings.detail: Path: Nov 2025 367.621, Dec 381.094, Mar 2026 406.965, Apr 418.952, Aug 469.251. The record is per Trading Economics. Computed: 469.251/367.621 = +27.6%; 469.251/711.611 = 65.9% of peak. There is no BLS PPI for grain-oriented electrical steel; cold-rolled carbon sheet is only a sentiment proxy for core steel.

findings.claim: The PPI for hot-rolled steel bars, plates and structural shapes (WPU101704) rose to 312.467 in Aug 2026, +5.9% since Apr 2026, mostly in Jun-Jul.
findings.detail: Apr 295.116, May 296.030, Jun 301.912, Jul 312.161, Aug 312.467. The seasonally adjusted WPS101704 was 286.972 in Nov 2025. The pure carbon-plate series WPU10170403 was discontinued in May 2017. Steel mill products (WPU1017) were 381.162 and iron and steel (WPU101) 378.128 in Aug 2026. Plate goes into tanks, so this matters for power-transformer tank cost.

findings.claim: Cleveland-Cliffs reported a domestic HRC average of $980/net ton in Q1 2026 (+24% YoY) and a Q2 2026 average selling price of $1,124/net ton.
findings.detail: The Q1 figure is from the Q1 2026 10-Q (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000764065/000076406526000070/clf-20260331.htm). Q2 steel shipments fell 6%. Neither filing excerpt disclosed GOES-specific pricing.

findings.claim: No government price index exists for grain-oriented electrical steel. Public anchors are a DLA contract ceiling of about $7,547/short ton, a weak tracker estimate of about $3,890/short ton for North America, and Cliffs' 2024 GOES raw-material surcharge of $375-465/net ton.
findings.detail: Computed: $400M / 53,000 short tons = $7,547/st. The DLA sole-source contract (Jul 2026, through Sep 8, 2030) is a ceiling, not a unit price (https://www.kallanish.com/en/news/steel/market-reports/article-details/cleveland-cliffs-secures-major-grain-oriented-electrical-steel-contract-0726/). $4.29/kg x 907.185 = about $3,892/short ton. Cliffs surcharge sheet (Feb 2024): https://d1io3yog0oux5.cloudfront.net/_ae56a054eb1e4fcd67e852eae3214501/clevelandcliffs/files/pages/clevelandcliffs/db/1185/description/2024-02-Surch-ES.pdf. GTAIC import-price averages (Europe $2.42k/t, world narrow $3.19k/t) are not US data.

findings.claim: CRS (Apr 23, 2026) reports that DOE found transformer price increases correlated with GOES prices starting in 2021, that imported electrical-steel articles have faced 50% tariffs since Aug 15, 2025, and that the US imports about 25-30% of distribution transformers, mainly from Taiwan, Canada and Mexico.
findings.detail: The same report says BLS data show distribution and large power transformer prices up about 40% from 2020 to 2024 after adjusting for inflation. Policy options it covers: extending 45X to distribution transformers (S.448/H.R.4128), reserving 48C funds, a government purchase quota with a buyer-of-last-resort backstop, and DPA Title III.

findings.claim: Cleveland-Cliffs says its Butler Works induction reheat furnace upgrade, which adds about 25% to grain-oriented output, completes in 2028.
findings.detail: This adds timing (2028) to the baseline's 'up to +25%'. The domestic GOES supply relief therefore lands after 2027, so an entrant starting production in 2027 would still depend on imported GOES or cores carrying 50% Section 232 duties.

findings.claim: The aluminum mill shapes PPI (WPU102501) fell to 370.902 in Aug 2026 from 394.292 in Jun (-5.9%), while copper inputs hit records.
findings.detail: Jun 394.292, Jul 388.048, Aug 370.902. Computed: 370.902/394.292 = -5.9%. Aluminum is the main alternative winding conductor in distribution transformers. A widening copper-aluminum cost gap favors aluminum-wound designs.

findings.claim: The PPI for unfinished oils and lubricating-oil base stock (PCU324110324110J) more than doubled YoY to 834.337 in Aug 2026 (Aug 2025: 394.580), a record.
findings.detail: Monthly: Aug 2025 394.580, Sep 393.856, Oct 383.243, Nov 373.363, Dec 384.507, Jan 2026 348.891, Feb 356.573, Mar 359.343, Apr 419.307, May 657.439 (+56.8% MoM), Jul 837.367, Aug 834.337. Computed: YoY +111.4%; Jan to Aug +139%. This exceeds the prior record of 727.509 (Jul 2022, per TE). The index covers base stocks broadly, not naphthenic transformer oil specifically. Lubricating oils and greases (PCU3241913241910) were 767.926 in Aug 2026.

findings.claim: Ergon raised North American naphthenic prices, including HyVolt dielectric (transformer) fluids, four times in Mar-Apr 2026, for a cumulative +$2.05/gal.
findings.detail: Increases: +$0.45 (Mar 13), +$0.35 (Mar 27), +$0.55 (Apr 10), +$0.70 (Apr 17); the sum is computed. The releases cite Middle East developments (https://ergon.com/updates/). Lubes'N'Greases [S] reports Calumet +$0.35/gal (Mar 10) and Cross Oil +$0.45/gal (Mar 13), and notes pale-oil tightness driven by transformer-oil demand.

findings.claim: Fed G.17 capacity utilization for NAICS 335 was 85.85% in Aug 2026, in an 85.7-86.3% range since Mar 2026, about 10 points above total industry (76.3%).
findings.detail: Path: Nov 2024 85.37; Oct 2025 83.14; Nov 2025 83.67 (FRED release table https://fred.stlouisfed.org/release/tables?eid=50002&rid=13); Dec 2025 85.07; Jan 2026 84.99; Feb 85.21; Mar 86.02 (May 2026 vintage); Apr 85.89 (first print 86.27); May 86.32; Jun 85.73; Jul 85.95; Aug 85.85 (Sep 18 vintage). Total industry was 76.3% in Aug 2026 (Fed). Manufacturing was about 75.5% in Feb 2026 against a long-run average of 78.0% (YCharts, S).

findings.claim: Industrial production for NAICS 3353 electrical equipment (IPG3353S) was flat at about 96-98 (2017=100) through H1 2026, i.e. still below its 2017 level.
findings.detail: Feb 2026 96.2148, Mar 95.85, Apr 97.9936, May 97.3455, Jun 96.9696. Jul and Aug were not retrieved. NAICS 3353 includes transformers plus motors, generators, switchgear, relays and controls, so it is not transformer-only. Its relative importance weight was 0.7181% of total IP in Mar 2026 (RIWG3353S).

findings.claim: The Fed's capacity index for NAICS 335 was 116.85 in Jul 2026 (2017 output=100). With 85.95% utilization, that implies NAICS 335 output of about 100.4, roughly its 2017 level.
findings.detail: Computed: 116.8543 x 0.859466 = 100.43. High utilization coexists with flat output. The Fed's annual revision (fed-g17-revision) will re-benchmark capacity using QPC data through Q4 2025.

findings.claim: The Fed's May 2026 G.17 release appears to show NAICS 335 output down 0.2% in 2025 but rising 6.7% annualized in Q4 2025 and 7.1% in Q1 2026, with Apr 2026 up about 4.5% YoY.
findings.detail: Tagged S rather than P because the search tool read garbled table text and column alignment could not be confirmed. Verify in the G.17 PDF or the Data Download Program.

findings.claim: The Fed plans its annual G.17 revision for Nov 24, 2026. It moves to a 2022 base year and revises capacity using Census QPC data through Q4 2025 plus USGS and DOE capacity data.
findings.detail: Capacity and utilization levels for NAICS 335/3353 may shift materially after this date. Re-pull the series after Nov 24.

findings.claim: MISO's MTEP26 cost guide escalates most transmission costs 4% per year but applies a higher rate to power transformers, breakers and disconnect switches. MISO's MTEP25 response cited 8% per year for substation equipment from 2024.
findings.value: 4% base; >4% for power transformers; 8% substation equipment (MTEP25)
findings.detail: MTEP24 used 5%. MTEP25 response: https://cdn.misoenergy.org/PSC%20Transmission%20Cost%20Estimation%20Guide%20for%20MTEP25%20Response%20(20250306)698318.pdf. Entergy argued that historical factors miss tariff and volatility effects; MISO added a 'Market Uncertainty' category. The exact MTEP26 transformer rate (Table 2.3-7) was not retrieved. Planners are budgeting transformer inflation at or above the 7-9% PPI pace.

findings.claim: Published measures of transformer price inflation since 2019-20 vary widely: BLS WPU117409 +91% nominal (Jan 2020-Jul 2026), WoodMac +77% (vs 2019, baseline), CRS about +40% real (2020-24), and anecdotal claims of up to 400% or 5-6x for small buyers.
findings.detail: The 400% figure is from CRS Insight IN12048 (https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IN/PDF/IN12048/IN12048.2.pdf). The 5-6x figure is from an NREL/OSTI report and is undefined. I trust the BLS index for transactions-weighted producer prices. Spot quotes for small, urgent buyers can run far above the index. PPI measures producer transaction prices, not quotes.

findings.claim: BLS no longer publishes a distribution-vs-power transformer product split: the industry product series PCU3353113353111 ended in Feb 2023, and BLS removed about 350 more PPIs effective with Jan 2026 data.
findings.detail: The list of discontinued indexes was not visible in search, so whether transformer series were among the Jan 2026 cuts is unconfirmed. The FRED date range for PCU3353113353111 ends 2023-02. The only current transformer splits are WPU117409 (power and distribution) vs WPU117411 (other and parts).

findings.claim: Canada's Industrial Product Price Index rose 13.5% YoY and 1.3% MoM in Aug 2026. StatCan begins a sample transition with the Sep 2026 reference month.
findings.detail: A transformer product class exists (NAPCS 38122, power, distribution and other transformers and parts; https://www23.statcan.gc.ca/imdb/p3VD.pl?Function=getVD&TVD=1254983&CVD=1255025&CPV=381222&CST=01012017&CLV=4&MLV=5), but its values in table 18-10-0266-01 were not retrieved. September IPPI is due Oct 22, 2026.

findings.claim: Mexico's INPP for secondary activities rose 3.72% YoY in May 2026. INEGI bulletins do not break out transformers.
findings.detail: The total INPP rose +2.98% YoY in May 2026. The electricity generation/T&D/water/gas group fell -6.08% YoY in Sep 2026. A transformer class (SCIAN 3353 generics) would need INEGI's BIE database.

result.analysis:
For someone thinking about building transformers, the government data show five things.

1. Pricing power is intact and picking up again. All four transformer PPIs hit records in Jul-Aug 2026. YoY growth roughly doubled, from about 4% in June to 7.6-8.7% (ppi-momentum-reaccel, ppi-wpu117409-jul26, ppi-335311-aug26, ppi-wpu1174-aug26). That contradicts the baseline's "decelerating" label. The path is a staircase, though:
   - Oct'25 to Jun'26 was a soft patch (ppi-335311-softpatch).
   - July brought a single +4.0% to +4.6% step, and August was flat (ppi-wpu117409-staircase).
   - Model prices as periodic resets, not a smooth trend. September data lands Oct 15. Note that WPU117409 printed no August value (ppi-wpu117409-aug-missing), and the baseline's Jan'26 figure has been revised down (ppi-wpu117409-revisions).

2. The 2026 step-up is mostly costs being passed through, and input inflation is running far ahead of output prices.
   - Copper: LME +45% to +48% YoY (cu-lme-yoy); copper wire PPI about +19% YoY and +13% since April (cu-wire-ppi).
   - Steel: cold-rolled sheet +28% since Nov'25 (steel-cold-rolled).
   - Oil: base-stock PPI +111% YoY (oil-baseoil-ppi); Ergon has taken $2.05/gal on transformer fluids (oil-ergon).
   - With output prices up only 7-9%, makers with fixed-price backlogs are likely seeing margin squeeze.
   - An entrant should quote with copper, GOES and oil escalators and hedge copper on LME. The COMEX premium has collapsed, so LME is a fair proxy (cu-comex-premium).
   - Aluminum is easing (aluminum-ppi), which favors aluminum-wound distribution designs.
   - GOES has no public price index at all (goes-pricing), and Cliffs' +25% GOES capacity arrives only in 2028 (cliffs-goes-capacity). This is the biggest unhedgeable input risk.

3. The gap between domestic and import prices is widening. The duty-exclusive BLS import index for NAICS 335 is flat YoY, while domestic transformer PPIs are up about 8% and switchgear 13% (mxp-iz335-flat, mxp-excl-duties, ppi-switchgear). The gap is largely the tariff wedge: 50% on electrical steel articles since Aug'25 (goes-crs). That helps the case for domestic plants, but it depends on policy, and there is no transformer-specific import index to watch (mxp-hs8504-stale).

4. Do not underwrite on the 2021-22 surge. Most of the +91% since 2020 came in 2021-22 (ppi-history-mpsc, ppi-history-dec). From 2023 to mid-2025 the index rose only about 3-7% a year (ppi-annual-2023-2025, ppi-plateau-check). CRS estimates the real increase at about 40% over 2020-24 (price-measures-conflict). A base case of mid-single-digit nominal price growth plus cost pass-through is defensible. MISO planners already budget more than 4%, and around 8%, for substation equipment (miso-escalation).

5. Capacity is tight but not expanding output. NAICS 335 utilization has held at 85.7-86.3% in 2026, about 10 points above all industry, while NAICS 3353 output is flat and below its 2017 level (cu-335-util, ip-3353, cap-335). The Fed's Nov 24 revision may move these numbers (fed-g17-revision).

Key gaps: there is no current PPI splitting distribution from power transformers (bls-detail-cuts), no GOES index, and Census QPC rates for NAICS 3353 were not retrievable here.

The second half (that the constraint cannot be upgraded with government or NEMA data) is refuted by these sources:
(1) The DOE LPT Resilience Report to Congress, signed Jul 10, 2024 (energy.gov/sites/default/files/2024-10/EXEC-2022-001242...pdf) [P], gives the 89% and 66% figures from the 2020 Commerce survey of 87 domestic LPT component manufacturers. Caveat: the survey is from 2020.

(3) The NIAC June 2024 transformer report (cisa.gov) [P] says the industry has had difficulty attracting and retaining workers.
(4) The BLS OEWS 51-2021 pages (bls.gov/oes/2023/may/oes512021.htm, plus the 2022 and 2020 editions) [P] give the occupation figures above.
(5) The BLS NAICS 335 overview page (bls.gov/iag/tgs/iag335.htm) [P] gives the 2025 coil winder wages ($23.44/hr median, $23.88/hr mean; $48,740 and $49,680 a year). It also gives NAICS 335 CES employment of 439.5k (Jun 2026) and 446.3k (Sep 2026, preliminary).

(8) Niskanen, via Manufacturing mag and E&E News [S/W], says US transformer manufacturing employs about 15,000 people and would need roughly to triple.

The data cuts both ways. Coil-winder headcount in NAICS 3353 fell and wages rose about 15%, which fits a tight market. A plausible reading is that the constraint is about trainability and experience, not posted pay.

result.analysis:
This run produced no new primary government data. The shared WebSearch budget for the turn (200 calls across all agents) was already spent when this agent started, so the first call was refused. The tool notice and the task rules (no WebFetch or curl) also ruled out any workaround. The QCEW, Census (Economic Census 2022, CBP, ASM/AIES) and plant-hiring targets remain open. The gaps list gives exact series, URLs and filters so a follow-up turn can fill them quickly.

What the baseline already holds can be organized into a labor-demand picture. All of it is computed, and it confirms rather than extends the baseline. Sourced announcements commit about 5,731 US jobs across 13 projects, plus 500 in Quebec (announced-us-jobs-total). Those jobs are concentrated in NC (1,106), AL (1,100), MS (800), TX (800) and SC (700) (announced-jobs-by-state). Timing is back-loaded: about 1,589 jobs at plants due in 2027, 1,100 in 2028 and 700 in 2029 (announced-jobs-timing). Labor demand therefore peaks just as the 2027-29 capacity wave lands. A greenfield entrant hiring in 2027-28 in the Southeast would be bidding for the same coil winders, testers and assemblers as Siemens, Eaton, Prolec, VTC and Hitachi. That pushes toward sites outside these clusters, or toward a rewind/remanufacturing shop that trains its own winders first, as the baseline's aftermarket thesis already suggests.

Capex per announced job ranges from about $0.10M (VTC Rincon, a brownfield expansion) to $1.0M (Howard Ellisville), with a median of about $0.47M (capex-per-announced-job). Adding lines and shifts in an existing plant buys far more labor-driven output per dollar than a greenfield or test-bay-heavy plant. That fits the baseline's point that incumbents' brownfield moves are fast and hard to undercut.

The key test this domain was meant to run is still open: is real industry headcount actually rising? QCEW 335311 employment and establishment counts from 2019 to 2026 Q1 separate announced capacity from capacity that is staffed and producing. If national 335311 employment grew strongly since 2022 in TN, VA, NC and MS, supply is responding, and the narrowing deficit WoodMac reports (15% in 2026) is credible. If it is flat, announcements are running ahead of execution, and the shortage window for an entrant is longer than the baseline implies.

The labor-shortage claim itself is still unproven (labor-constraint-unquantified). Six of the ten target plants have no job figure in the baseline (target-plants-missing-hiring-data). The highest-value next pulls are QCEW 335311 quarterly slices, OEWS wages for SOC 51-2021 and 51-2028, CES series for NAICS 3353, and state workforce-board partnerships at the named plants.

result.analysis:
I have no new permit evidence to report. When this subagent started, the session's shared WebSearch budget (200 calls per turn across all agents) was already used up. All four searches I sent came back unexecuted: MDEQ/Gallman, ADEM/Virginia Transformer, Shelby County/Hyosung and ADEM/HD Hyundai. The container also blocks direct fetches, and the harness says not to route around the limit, so I did not try to. The findings list is empty on purpose. I have not confirmed, updated or contradicted any baseline figure, and every number in the table comes from the baseline, not from a permit.

What I did produce is a permit-retrieval checklist built from the baseline. For a would-be transformer builder, these checks matter most:

1. **Schedule risk on the plants that set the 2027-29 supply wave.** The baseline puts HD Hyundai Montgomery #2 at Apr 2027, Eaton Jonesville at 2027, Virginia Transformer Muscle Shoals at Jan 2028 and Hitachi Gallman at 2029. Muscle Shoals is a 600k sq ft greenfield plant announced 2026-05-19 with production promised about 20 months later, so it has the shortest runway. Gallman was announced only on 2026-09-15. If neither has an air construction permit or NPDES construction stormwater coverage yet, the incumbents' capacity arrives later than the baseline assumes. That would leave a new entrant a longer window of tight supply.

2. **Real output ceilings.** Air permits for transformer plants usually cap VOC from varnish, paint and impregnation, and the throughput of drying ovens and vapor-phase dryers. Those caps turn press-release claims into a hard upper bound. Examples are Hyosung's "130 to 250+ units/yr" and Hitachi's "more than doubles" its US 10-160 MVA output. The existing Crystal Springs permit is the natural baseline against which to size Gallman.

3. **Unverified sites.** The baseline still lists Central Moloney Panama City Beach as "unverified start" and gives Howard Ellisville no online date. A certificate of occupancy or a state air registration would settle both.

Recommended next step: send a follow-up message, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION, then work the table row by row. Use allowed_domains for mdeq.ms.gov, adem.alabama.gov, epd.georgia.gov, shelbycountytn.gov, tn.gov, des.sc.gov, deq.louisiana.gov and floridadep.gov in extended mode, plus local outlets for groundbreaking and progress news. Until that happens, treat the baseline online dates as company guidance that no permit record has verified.

No new primary data was retrieved for this domain. WebSearch refused every query: the workflow's shared budget of 200 searches per turn was already used up by other agents before this agent ran. Egress policy blocks direct fetches, and the instructions forbid working around that, so this output holds no new findings. To fill this domain, rerun it as a follow-up turn with fresh search budget, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION.

What the local review showed. The baseline (market-map.md, capacity_expansions.csv) contains no incentive, abatement, wage-floor or clawback data. It also has no capex figure for five of the 29 capacity rows: VTC Muscle Shoals, ERMCO Arizona, JST Wytheville, Giga Houston and VanTran Waco. These are the projects where local abatement or IDA filings usually state capex, because the abatement is calculated on it. The monitoring runbook (MONITORING.md) sweeps only governor press releases, not board minutes or incentive agreements. That gap is systematic, not a one-off.

Why this domain matters to someone entering transformer manufacturing:
1. Incentive agreements are contracts. Their performance dates (JDIG performance years, VEDP COF deadlines, EDGE PILOT terms, Union County FILOT investment periods) show when each incumbent has committed to hire and invest. They test whether the 2027–29 capacity wave in the baseline is contractually backed or aspirational. The baseline already records one slip (Siemens Charlotte, 2026 to 2027). An amended JDIG agreement would show whether that slip changed the contracted milestones.
2. The filings settle conflicts the baseline flags: the Hyosung $157–221M capex range (EDGE PILOT staff reports split real and personal property) and Giga's 1,000 vs 3,000+ unit target.
3. An IDA application such as Niagara's in Cheektowaga or a FILOT ordinance splits building cost from equipment cost. That split is the closest public benchmark for capex per unit of capacity in a brownfield expansion, which an entrant needs for its own model.
4. Award sizes per job across MS, AL, VA, NC, SC, TN and TX show which states pay most to win a transformer plant. That is a direct input to site selection and entry economics.
5. Agreements name the legal entity and parent. That bears on domestic-status questions under EO 14420 (for example JST, whose ownership the baseline flags as unverified) and on whether incentives carry change-of-control clauses (Delta Star under MacLean).

3. ECIDA or Cheektowaga IDA packets (Niagara).

findings.correction: PD No. 2026-10 of Apr 20, 2026 = FR Doc 2026-08013, 91 FR 21931 (published Apr 23, 2026). FR Doc 2026-08011 is a different determination, PD No. 2026-09 at 91 FR 21929. Correct URL: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-04-23/pdf/2026-08013.pdf
findings.verify_evidence:
The substance holds but the citation is wrong. Federal Register and govinfo [P] list Presidential Determination No. 2026-10 of April 20, 2026, the section 303 DPA determination 'on Grid Infrastructure, Equipment, and Supply Chain Capacity', as FR Doc 2026-08013 at 91 FR 21931, published April 23, 2026 and addressed to the Secretary of Energy. The same day's Federal Register lists FR Doc 2026-08011 as PD No. 2026-09 (section 303, large-scale energy and energy-related infrastructure, 91 FR 21929-21930). FR Doc 2026-08010 (91 FR 21927) is also a different document. The coal determination, PD 2026-08, was published that day too. The baseline error is in /home/user/claude-shit/transformer-market/dashboard/build_data.py line 152, which links 2026-08011.pdf.

The content is confirmed. The determination finds that 'grid infrastructure and its associated upstream supply chains, including transformers, transmission lines and conductors, substations, high-voltage circuit breakers, power control electronics, protective relay systems, capacitor banks, electrical core steel, and related raw materials and manufacturing tools' are essential to the national defense under section 303(a)(5). It cites the EO 14156 energy emergency and waives section 303(a)(1)-(a)(6) under 303(a)(7). It authorizes the Secretary of Energy to make 'purchases, commitments, and financial instruments'. So the Title III purchase and financing framing is accurate.

Independent checks for a Title III award or solicitation under this determination found none. I searched energy.gov, grants.gov, simpler.grants.gov, sam.gov and federalregister.gov. The only public DOE implementation step found is a June 15, 2026 RFI (FR Doc 2026-11971, docket EERE-2026-BT-STD-0133, comments due July 15, 2026). It asks whether the 2024 distribution transformer efficiency standards (compliance April 23, 2029) reduce the ability to surge production. It also asks for suggestions on implementing PD 2026-10, and it confirms that transformers and electrical core steel are covered. This supports the baseline's 'no award yet' point.

NEW RISK the finding omits: most DPA authorities, Title III included, were set by the FY2026 NDAA (P.L. 119-60) to sunset on September 30, 2026 (CRS R49178, Aug 13, 2026 [P]). H.R. 7688, the DPA Modernization Act of 2026, would extend them to September 30, 2031. It passed the House by voice vote on September 16, 2026 (congress.gov [P]). I found no evidence of Senate passage or enactment by October 11, 2026. Whether DOE can start new Title III actions under PD 2026-10 is therefore UNVERIFIED and may be suspended by a lapse. The baseline's 'In force' status should be qualified.

findings.verify_evidence:
The core facts are confirmed [P]. The Cleveland-Cliffs release (Business Wire and clevelandcliffs.com news release #704) says Cliffs would host Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Assistant Secretary Audrey Robertson and Under Secretary of Commerce William Kimmitt at Butler Works on Tuesday, October 6. It describes 'Cleveland-Cliffs' $200 million investment in Butler Works, supported by a $75 million award from the U.S. Department of Energy' and says the project will 'expand the facility's GOES production volume by up to 25 percent'. The release is dated October 5, 2026; the Business Wire ID reads 20261004, so the baseline's as_of of 2026-10-04 is one day early. Butler Eagle (Oct 6, 2026 [S]) and SteelOrbis (Oct 7 [S]) confirm the visit took place.

The unverified lead in the finding is CONFIRMED. The $75M is the DOE Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations Industrial Demonstrations Program (IDP) selection. It is not money from the April 2026 DPA determination. Evidence for this:
- Cliffs' March 25, 2024 release [P]: 'Butler Works Induction Reheat Furnaces (up to $75 million grant)', part of $575M across two projects (the other is up to $500M at Middletown).
- DOE IDP selection briefing [P]: 'Steel Slab Electrified Induction Reheat Furnace Upgrade', Lyndora, PA.
- DOE 'Award Wednesdays' (Aug 21, 2024) and the IDP fact sheet [P]: more than $19M awarded for Phase 1 (planning, permitting and design) out of a federal cost share of up to $75M. The remainder is subject to future negotiation.
- BlueGreen Alliance (Mar 25, 2024 [S]).
- Butler Eagle (Oct 6, 2026 [S]): the grant 'was awarded in March 2024 under the Biden administration' and passed review by the Trump administration earlier in 2026. Asst. Sec. Robertson said the Biden criteria centered on decarbonization. So this is a retained decarbonization grant that has been reframed around GOES and national security, not new DPA money.

Corrections to the finding's detail:
(1) The completion date IS disclosed. The Oct 5, 2026 release says 'early 2028'. The DOE IDP project page and Cliffs filings say 2029. DOE's 2024 fact sheet targeted hot commissioning in Q2 2027 and completion in Q2 2028. These sources conflict. Trust the 2026 company release for the current target, and treat 2029 as DOE's contractual date.
(2) The output effect conflicts. Cliffs says GOES volume rises by up to 25% (2026 release). DOE's 2024 materials cited an expected 12.5% increase in GOES shipments from better slab quality. Cliffs' DEF 14A of Apr 2, 2026 speaks of 30-40% more GOES tonnage from existing capacity. Treat 25% as a company ceiling, not a DOE-validated figure.
(3) The $75M is 'up to' a cost-share ceiling. I found no primary source showing Phase 2 negotiations finalized or the full amount obligated: Cliffs' 2025 annual report says negotiations with DOE continued through 2025, and a USAspending search returned nothing.

Other details: the induction reheat furnaces are made in Warren, OH, and peak construction employment is about 220 (Butler Eagle). Separately, on Aug 21, 2026 Cliffs said DOE set a framework to rescope its $500M Middletown IDP grant [P], which is evidence that IDP grants are being repurposed rather than cancelled. I found nothing on the ~920 mm GOES width limit.

result.analysis:
This run added NO new primary data. The shared WebSearch budget for this workflow turn (200 calls across all agents) was used up before this agent's first query, and per the harness instruction I did not route around it with curl, wget or proxies. Everything below is restated from the local baseline, each item with its original URL, plus a queue of clearly labeled, unverified leads. To continue, send a follow-up message (which resets the per-turn budget) or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION.

What the existing evidence implies for someone building transformers:

1. The legal tool exists, but no money for transformer makers is visible yet. PD 2026-10 (dpa-pd-2026-10) lets DOE use DPA Title III purchases and financing for transformers, grid equipment and core steel. Neither the baseline nor any source checked shows a Title III award, offtake commitment or solicitation for a transformer assembler. A builder should not put DPA money into a base-case model until a solicitation appears in the Federal Register or on SAM.gov. If one does appear, it is the federal lever most likely to favor a new US entrant, because Title III can fund capacity and guarantee purchases.

2. The only visible federal dollars go to inputs, through an incumbent. The $75M DOE award at Cleveland-Cliffs Butler Works (cliffs-butler-doe-75m) supports up to 25% more GOES. Which program it comes from is unconfirmed: one unverified lead is a 2024 OCED Industrial Demonstrations Program grant, not new DPA money. If confirmed, the 2026 federal push is so far rhetoric plus repurposed grants. Either way, the GOES bottleneck (one domestic maker, narrow widths) stays the gating risk for a new plant.

3. The 48C tax credit may no longer be available. If the unverified lead that the ~$10B 48C cap was fully allocated by early 2025 is right, a 2026-27 entrant cannot count on a 30% investment credit. State incentives (not covered here) become the main non-dilutive capital source.

4. Federal procurement could serve as a reference customer. BPA, WAPA, TVA, USACE and Reclamation buy GSUs and substation units under domestic-content rules. The EO 14420 rules (eo14420-doe-rfi, due about Dec 24) may tighten eligibility further. No award values or lead times were retrieved. The procurement table lists the exact USAspending and SAM.gov pulls (PSC 6120/5950, NAICS 335311, FY25-26 by sub-agency) to run next.

Bottom line: for now, treat federal support as upside, not base case. The next run should first check for (a) any Title III solicitation and (b) USAspending FY25-26 PSC 6120 vendor and origin data.
