findings.claim: The baseline's 50% Section 232 rate on imported GOES transformer cores and laminations rests only on a social-media post, and market-map.md states no rate at all, so the duty a new builder would pay on imported cores is unverified.
findings.detail: Audit of the local baseline, not a new search result. dashboard/build_data.py line 147 records the row 'Section 232 steel derivatives: cores and laminations' as in force since Aug 18, 2025 at 50%, with an X/Twitter post as its source, tagged W. market-map.md section 7 says only 'Covered by steel 232 since 2025'. The baseline does not say which HTS lines (8504.90 parts, or GOES strip under 7225.11/7226.11) carry which rate after the April 2026 restructure under Proclamation 11021. Many entrants plan to import cores, so whether that duty is 25% or 50% of full customs value is a first-order cost question. Check against the Proclamation 11021 annex and CBP CSMS before modelling.
findings.correction: 25% of full customs value (Section 232 Annex I-B) for imported laminations, stacked cores and wound cores (HTS 8504.90.9634 / .9638 / .9642), with no Annex III 15% reduction. The baseline's 50% figure is not supported for cores. GOES strip itself (Chapter 72, 7225.11 / 7226.11) is reportedly in the 50% Annex I-A tier, but the specific lines were not confirmed.
findings.verify_evidence:
AUDIT PART: CONFIRMED locally. build_data.py line 147 gives 50%, tag W, source an X post. market-map.md section 7 says only 'Covered by steel 232 since 2025', with no rate.

SUBSTANCE: the duty can now be checked against primary text, and 50% is wrong for cores.
(1) The June 2026 White House Annex I-B, titled '25% Section 232 Tariff on Full Value', lists 8504.90.9634 (laminations for stacked cores), 8504.90.9638 (stacked cores) and 8504.90.9642 (wound cores) [P]. The April 2026 combined annex PDF lists the same three codes. Its file title reads '50%', but its note says a 25% rate applies to the full value [P]. That inconsistency may be where a 50% claim came from.
(2) The Annex III temporary reduction list carries a transformer-parts line, 8504.90.9646, 'Parts for electrical transformers, nesoi (excluding laminations and cores)'. Cores therefore do NOT get the 15% tier [P].
(3) Secondary sources say Chapter 72 steel, which includes GOES strip, sits in the 50% Annex I-A tier. I could not see the 7225.11 / 7226.11 rows in the annex text, so 50% for GOES strip is plausible but not line-confirmed.
(4) Goods subject to Section 232 are excluded from the Jul 24, 2026 Section 301 forced-labor tariff (USTR fact sheet [P]; CBP Forced Labor HTS list [P]). Imported cores therefore pay 232 plus MFN only, with no 301 adder.
(5) Proclamation 11032 (Jun 2026) cut the 'entirely US-melted metal' threshold for the lower tier from 95% to 85% (FR 2026-11314 [P]). That bears on cores made from US-melted GOES.
(6) One law-firm summary (Holland & Knight, via a search snippet) says Ch. 84/85 parts imported only to manufacture Annex III fixed industrial equipment can get a reduced tiered rate. I could not verify this or its interaction with the cores exclusion before the search budget ran out.

The Aug 18, 2025 start date in the baseline was not re-verified.

Line 160 sources the Dec 31, 2027 expiry to GHY, a customs broker (S). HTS 8504.23 covers liquid-dielectric transformers above 10,000 kVA. HTS 8504.34 covers other (dry) transformers above 500 kVA. These are standard HTSUS headings, not re-checked this run. Under the narrow reading, liquid distribution units of 10,000 kVA or less (8504.21, 8504.22) and small dry-type units (8504.31-.33) stay at 25%. Imported large power units would then pay 10 points less duty than imported distribution units. That favours a domestic distribution or pad-mount builder over a domestic LPT builder. The scope has not been confirmed from the Proclamation text.
findings.correction: Annex III (primary) lists 8504.23.00 and 8504.34.00 (plus some 8504.90 parts, excluding cores and laminations). The 15% is a COMBINED cap: Column 1 MFN plus Section 232 equals 15%, and 232 adds 0% if MFN is already 15% or more. It has applied since Apr 6, 2026 under Proclamation 11021 clause (5); Proclamation 11032 (signed Jun 1, effective Jun 8, 2026) expanded it. It expires Dec 31, 2027, after which these lines revert to the 25% Annex I-B rate. 8504.21, 8504.22, 8504.32 and 8504.33 are on Annex I-B at 25% of full value.
findings.verify_evidence:

SUBSTANCE: the narrow scope now has primary support. The June 2026 White House Annex III ('Temporary Reduction List for Section 232 Steel and Aluminum Derivatives') includes 8504.23.00 (liquid dielectric, >10,000 kVA) and 8504.34.00 (non-liquid, >500 kVA). Its note says the 25% tariff is reduced 'until December 31, 2027' under clause (5) of Proclamation 11021 [P]. The June 2026 Annex I-B lists 8504.21.00, 8504.22.00, 8504.32 and 8504.33.00 at 25% of full value [P]. One caveat: the extracted annex text is partly garbled, so the 8504.34 description should be read off the PDF.

Details to correct:
(a) START DATE. The tier began Apr 6, 2026. An AFS Law alert from April 2026 [S] describes Annex III as 48 codes (35 steel, 13 aluminum) covering 'metal-intensive industrial and electrical grid equipment' at a combined 15%. A Utility Dive article from April 2026 [S] reports the 15% grid-equipment rate as part of the Apr 6 restructure. Troutman [S] says Proclamation 11032 (effective Jun 8) widened the tier from 'fixed industrial machinery and power equipment' to agricultural equipment and residential HVAC. The dashboard's 2026-06-08 date is therefore the amendment date, not the start date.
(b) RATE MECHANICS. 15% is total duty including MFN, not 15% added on top of MFN (AFS Law; Proclamation 11032 text at FR 2026-11314) [P/S].
(c) THE ~10-POINT GAP (computed). Annex I-B units pay 25% plus MFN; Annex III units pay 15% in total. The 2013/2014 HTS editions show 8504.23 MFN at 1.6% [P, but not confirmed for 2026]. One vendor says 8504.22 MFN is Free [W]. If 8504.22 is Free, the gap is 25 - 15 = 10 points. If it is 1.6%, the gap is 26.6 - 15 = 11.6 points.
(d) WHAT THE NARROW SCOPE COVERS. 8504.23 is 'above 10 MVA'. That covers medium power (10-160 MVA) as well as LPTs, so the 15% tier helps imports competing with Hitachi Gallman or VTC, not only EHV units.

Unresolved: one search fragment placed 8504.23.00 near the Annex I-A section of the April combined PDF, which is probably a text-extraction artifact. CBP CSMS #68855869 (Jun 5, 2026) implements Proclamation 11032, but I could not retrieve its transformer-specific rows.

findings.detail: Audit of the local baseline. market-map.md section 7 says 'Mexico 10% (USMCA goods possibly exempt)'. build_data.py line 156 says 'Mexico 10% (non-USMCA goods)'. findings.verify_evidence:
AUDIT PART: CONFIRMED locally. market-map.md section 7 says 'USMCA goods possibly exempt'. build_data.py line 156 says '10% (non-USMCA goods)'.

SUBSTANCE: both baseline readings miss the decisive exclusion.
(1) USTR's Jul 23, 2026 fact sheet lists 'all articles and parts of articles subject to section 232 tariffs' as not covered [P].
(2) CBP's Forced Labor HTS list (attached to CSMS #69326983, Jul 23, 2026) says the 9903.05.20-.84 duties do not apply to articles under Section 232 headings 9903.82.02 and 9903.82.04-.26 [P].
(3) Honigman's own alert-3462, the source both baseline rows cite, says Section 232 articles (steel, aluminum, copper) are exempt and that goods entering duty-free under USMCA are exempt [S].
(4) Holland & Knight (Jul 27, 2026) agrees: USMCA-qualifying Mexican goods are excluded, and Section 232 goods are excluded but 'remain subject to their sectoral regimes... 25 to 50 percent' [S].

The dashboard's 'non-USMCA goods' is therefore right on USMCA, and market-map's 'possibly' is out of date. But the finding's line 'If not, 10 points stack on top', and the baseline's 'stacked on other duties / small adder on Korean and Mexican imports', are wrong for Section 232-covered transformers, which pay 232 plus MFN only.

Other checks:
- Dates: USTR final action signed Jul 23, effective Jul 24, 2026, published in the FR on Jul 28, 2026 (2026-15181, 2026-15274) [P].
- Korea: 12.5% net of MFN, confirmed [S].
- Canada (NEW, missing from the baseline): Section 338 duties of 50% on selected Canadian products, effective Aug 22, 2026. There is no USMCA exemption, but secondary sources say Section 232 goods are excluded [S]. That suggests Canadian-made transformers are unaffected; not confirmed against the proclamation.

findings.verify_evidence:
AUDIT PART: CONFIRMED locally. market-map section 7 says 'EEI wants a later compliance date; some makers want changes' with no link. The dashboard cites only DOE's RFI page.

Independent sources now support EEI's position, and they contradict the 'some makers want changes' part.
- RFI: FR doc 2026-11971 (Jun 15, 2026), docket EERE-2026-BT-STD-0133, comments due Jul 15, 2026 [P]. It was triggered by the Apr 20, 2026 DPA determination. DOE's page gives compliance as Apr 23, 2029; Howard says 'May 2029'.
- EEI (Jul 15): supports the 2024 rule and, rather than repeal, says members 'would benefit from longer compliance times' (Utility Dive [S]; the EEI document itself was not found, and it names no specific date).
- APPA: 'does not advocate for any changes' but wants amorphous-steel supply monitored [S].
- NRECA (Jul 14): the rule 'strikes the right balance' [S].
- NEMA (Jul 15): urges DOE not to disrupt the 2024 rule's certainty. It backs H.R. 4626 Sec. 3 to remove distribution transformers from EPCA review. It says there is one domestic GOES maker and that the only large-scale amorphous producer supplies just 2% of the distribution-transformer market [S, via docket snippets and Utility Dive].
- Howard Industries (Jul 15, docket item 0032) [P]: opposes changing the rule before 2029. It says it has committed more than $180M of capital tied to the rule, including $30M at Laurel and $50M at other sites. It says most lead times are now under 20 weeks. It notes Cliffs' Butler expansion targets power-transformer GOES, not distribution-transformer GOES. It asks for reimbursement if DOE changes the rule.
- ERMCO (Jul 13, docket item 0015): calls the rule 'reasonable, balanced, and achievable' [P].
- SCE: concerned about amorphous supply [S].
- Cleveland-Cliffs (Jul 15): SUPPORTS changes, to 'preserve utilization of GOES for all types of covered distribution transformers' [S].

So the push for changes comes from the GOES steelmaker and individual commenters. The transformer makers on record (Howard, ERMCO, NEMA) oppose changes. No DOE follow-up (NOPR, delay or withdrawal) was found through Oct 11, 2026. The baseline's gap is real but now closable.

Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/15/2026-11971/energy-conservation-program-energy-conservation-standards-for-distribution-transformers ; https://www.utilitydive.com/news/doe-mulls-changes-to-biden-era-transformer-rule-raising-utility-concerns/826440/ ; https://downloads.regulations.gov/EERE-2026-BT-STD-0133-0032/attachment_1.pdf ; https://downloads.regulations.gov/EERE-2026-BT-STD-0133-0015/attachment_1.pdf ; https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/distribution-transformers

result.analysis:
This run collected no new primary evidence. The 200-search per-turn web budget, shared by every agent in this workflow turn, was used up before this agent's first query ran. As the tool notice and task rules require, nothing was fetched through curl, WebFetch or reader services. To get the deep primary-source pass the user asked for, the user should send a follow-up message to start a new turn with a fresh budget, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION. The verification queue table lists the exact domains and facts to target.

Instead, this agent audited the baseline's policy layer. That audit matters for someone about to commit capital, because some of the tariff figures that most affect a manufacturing plan rest on weak sources or contradict each other:

1. **Core input cost is unverified.** The 50% Section 232 rate on imported GOES cores and laminations comes only from a social-media post, and market-map.md gives no rate at all (s232-cores-rate-weakly-sourced). A new builder will almost certainly import cores or GOES at first, since Cleveland-Cliffs is the only US maker and its strip is narrow. Whether that duty is 25% or 50% of full value changes unit economics directly. Verify this first.

2. **Large-vs-distribution tariff gap rests on a vendor blog.** The 15% temporary tier for 8504.23 and 8504.34 (s232-grid-tier-weakly-sourced) cites DistroForge. If correct, imported large power units pay 10 points less than imported distribution units until Dec 31, 2027. That would tilt the case toward building distribution and pad-mount units rather than large power units, which matches the baseline's segment advice, but it needs the annex text.

3. **Mexico exposure is unresolved.** The baseline contradicts itself on whether USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the 10% Section 301 forced-labor tariff (s301-mexico-usmca-inconsistent). Mexico appears to be the largest import source, though that share comes from an aggregator (mexico-import-share-source-weak). It is also home to Prolec GE, WEG and Hammond. The answer sets the price floor of the main non-Chinese competition. Rates for India, Vietnam, Turkey, Japan, Germany and Canada are missing, and these countries now matter given the Marsons India-to-North America JV.

4. **DOE dockets are the next decisive inputs.** DOE-HQ-2026-1123 closed Oct 9 with rules due around Dec 24 (doe-rfi-closed-rules-due). Its comments will show whether utilities and data-center groups pushed for data-center carve-outs and grandfathering, which would weaken the domestic tailwind, or for pre-qualified vendor lists, which could lock out new entrants unless they qualify early. The efficiency docket (doe-eff-eei-claim-unsourced) decides amorphous vs GOES and redesign capex. The baseline's EEI claim there has no link.

5. **Lower-stakes open items.** The EO number (eo-number-conflict-persists), the Section 122 appeal (sec122-appeal-status-stale) and the IEEPA refunds (ieepa-refund-status-unquantified) remain open. They matter less for the decision.

**Bottom line:** do not treat the baseline's tariff rates as settled inputs to a cost model. Re-run this domain with a fresh budget, in this order: Proclamation 11021 annex and CBP CSMS, then the USTR Section 301 notice, then the DOE-HQ-2026-1123 comments, then the EERE comments.

result.analysis:
No new evidence was collected for this domain. When this agent sent its first batch of five extended searches (council approvals, pad-mount bid awards, bid tabulations, APPA survey, NRECA survey), the harness refused all of them: the 200-call WebSearch budget for this turn, shared by every agent in the workflow, was already used up. Direct fetches are blocked by egress policy, and the harness says not to work around the limit, so none were tried. The findings array is empty on purpose. Nothing here should be read as a price or lead-time datapoint.

What this means for someone planning to build transformers: the baseline (market-map.md and indicators.csv) still has a serious hole. Its distribution-class numbers (pad-mount ~30-60 weeks, pole-mount ~26-40 weeks, easing to 26-38 weeks by Q4'26) come only from two weak [W] vendor trackers. Its price evidence is index-level only: BLS PPI WPU117409 +91% vs Jan 2020 and +8.7% YoY, and WoodMac's +77% vs 2019. There is no buyer-level evidence of what utilities actually pay per unit by class, which vendors win public bids, or whether quoted delivery times are getting shorter. Those three facts matter most for a new entrant's pricing, product mix (e.g. 3-phase pad-mount vs pole-mount vs 10-50 MVA substation units) and go-to-market (municipal and co-op bids vs IOU frame agreements). Until procurement records are pulled, read the baseline's 'distribution lead times easing' claim as unconfirmed.

The highest-value next step is the search plan in the tables section, priority-1 rows first: council and board award memos from municipal utilities with fast load growth (Santa Clara/Silicon Valley Power, Texas munis, Pacific Northwest PUDs, California munis and JPAs, Southeast munis near the new MS/AL/TN/GA plants), plus APPA, NRECA and CoBank surveys. Award memos usually carry vendor, unit price and 'weeks ARO' delivery, and often the prior contract price, which gives a 2023-24 vs 2025-26 trend. Federal awards (usaspending.gov / sam.gov for BPA, WAPA, TVA, USACE) record vendor location, which supports a domestic vs import split. CFE (Mexico) and OEB (Ontario) filings cover the rest of North America.

To unblock: re-run this domain in a fresh turn, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION, with 25-35 searches. The empty datapoint template table lists the fields to fill. A follow-up should explicitly mark (a) whether utility-quoted distribution lead times confirm or contradict the baseline's 26-60 week range, and (b) whether bid unit prices rose faster or slower than the PPI's +8.7% YoY.

findings.claim: The '~$10.5B for 100% of Prolec GE' in the baseline is a calculation (2 x $5.254B), not a reported figure. It ignores control premium and deal terms.
findings.detail: Inputs: $5.254B paid for Xignux's 50%, closed Feb 2, 2026, cited to the GEV Q2 2026 10-Q. Doubling it gives $10.508B. That price bought control of a 50/50 JV, so it may include a control premium, earn-outs or debt and cash adjustments. The purchase-price allocation in the 10-Q (goodwill, remeasurement gain on the previously held 50%) would give a better whole-company value. Read that note before using $10.5B as an exit comparable. The $5.254B was not re-read this run.
findings.correction: Replace the baseline's '~$10.5B implied for 100%' with GE Vernova's own purchase accounting: total preliminary purchase consideration of $9,656M for 100% = $5,254M cash for Xignux's 50% + $4,402M fair value of the 50% GEV already held [P, GEV Q2 2026 10-Q]. The headline price was $5.275B; the cash consideration booked was $5.254B.
findings.verify_evidence: I tried to refute this and could not. The GEV Q2 2026 10-Q (and the Q1 2026 10-Q) confirm the claim and the $5,254M cash figure, and the PPA note the finding recommended reading gives a better whole-company value. (1) Cash consideration was $5,254M, closed Feb 2, 2026. The preliminary purchase-consideration table is: cash $5,254M + fair value of previously held 50% equity interest $4,402M = total $9,656M. The total was unchanged between Q1 and Q2. (2) GEV says it set the fair value of the old 50% 'using the implied total equity value from the transaction price, adjusted for an assumed control premium'. That pre-tax remeasurement gain of $3,992M is booked in Other income (expense), net. So the filer itself states that the $5.254B price embeds a control premium, and the finding's main point holds. The implied control premium is computed, not reported: $5,254M / $4,402M - 1 = 19.4% on the 50% block. (3) Preliminary PPA (Q2): intangibles $4,172M (Q1 had $3,980M), current assets $1,654M (Q1 $1,597M), current liabilities $(1,078)M, non-current liabilities $(1,528)M, identifiable net assets $4,343M, goodwill $5,313M (Q1 $5,473M; $160M measurement-period reduction). About $400M of goodwill is tax-deductible. The allocation is to be finalized no later than Q1 2027. Cash acquired and debt assumed are not broken out, so I cannot split equity value from enterprise value. (4) On deal terms, I found no earn-out. The announced and closing-release headline price was $5.275B (Oct 21, 2025 announcement; Feb 2, 2026 close), funded ~50% cash and ~50% debt, with a $2.6B senior notes issue. The $21M gap to the $5.254B cash booked is presumably a closing adjustment; that is my inference and is not stated. (5) There is a nuance in the other direction. One search summary of GEV's Oct 2025 acquisition deck reported the price as 13.9x 2025E and 9.4x 2028E adjusted EBITDA before synergies. With deck EBITDA of about $0.8B (2025E) and $1.1B (2028E) for 100% of Prolec, those multiples only reconcile if the base is about 2 x $5.275B = $10.55B (my computation: 10.55/0.76 = 13.9x; 10.55/1.12 = 9.4x). So GEV's own marketing multiple appears to use the doubled figure, while its accounting values 100% at $9.656B. A second search could not re-confirm the 13.9x quote, so treat it as unconfirmed [S-]. (6) There is also useful new operating data. Prolec GE revenue was $859M in Q2 2026 and $1,344M from Feb 2 to Jun 30, 2026. Pre-tax income was $(57)M in Q2 and $(166)M year-to-date, depressed by inventory step-up and amortization; Q1 had a $71M inventory fair-value charge. GEV 2026 revenue guidance includes about $3.1B from Prolec GE, up from about $3.0B. The deck's 2025E figures were revenue $3.0B and adjusted EBITDA about $0.8B (~25% margin); 2026E was $3.4B and $0.9B. (7) The baseline repeats the $10.5B in market-map.md line 173 ('Implies ~$10.5B for 100%') and in dashboard/build_data.py line 205 ('Prolec GE was valued near $10.5B'). Both should be changed to the $9.656B PPA figure, with the $10.55B 'headline x2' shown only as the basis for GEV's quoted multiple.

findings.correction: IPO priced Feb 5, 2026 (closed Feb 6) at $27.00: base deal 56,000,000 shares = $1,512.0M gross (424B4), of which only 16,586,427 shares ($427.7M before expenses) were primary. With the full 8,400,000-share option (closed Feb 9), the total was 64,400,000 shares, about $1,738.8M gross (computed). Forgent received $491.8M net. The '$47 follow-on' was the second of three: $29.50 (priced Mar 26, closed Mar 30, 2026; 34.5M shares incl. option), $47.00 (priced May 28, closed Jun 1, 2026; 48,622,000 shares incl. option), and $49.00 (priced Jul 1, closed Jul 6, 2026; 43,650,000 shares).
findings.verify_evidence: The audit's sourcing point is CONFIRMED. The baseline cites Renaissance Capital in deals.csv and for the forgent_ipo figure, and an Oppenheimer page for the $47 figure (dashboard/build_data.py line 60); no SEC filing is cited. The prices hold up against primary filings, but the framing needs correcting. (1) The 424B4 offering table shows $27.000/share, $1,512,000,000 gross, $1.215/share underwriting discount ($68.04M), and $25.785/share and $427,681,020 proceeds to the company before expenses. Base shares were 16,586,427 from the company and 39,413,573 from Neos-controlled selling stockholders. (2) 8-K Ex. 99.2 (Feb 9, 2026): the underwriters' option was exercised in full, adding 2,487,964 company shares and 5,912,036 selling-holder shares, for 64.4M shares in total. 64.4M x $27 = $1,738.8M (my computation). The baseline's '$1.5-1.7B' is therefore the base vs. greenshoe gross deal size. Most of it went to Neos-controlled sellers, so calling it '$1.5-1.7B raised' overstates what Forgent raised: $491.8M net per its 10-Q, and that was used to redeem Opco interests held by Neos entities. (3) Follow-ons, all per Forgent press releases on businesswire.com and forgentpower.com, its 10-Q and its FY2026 10-K. #1 priced Mar 26, 2026 at $29.50, base 30.0M shares (9,311,126 company + 20,688,874 sellers), with the full option for 34.5M total, closed Mar 30; 34.5M x $29.50 = about $1.02B (computed). #2 priced May 28, 2026 at $47.00, upsized, closed Jun 1, 2026 with the full option: 15,852,319 company + 32,769,681 Neos shares = 48,622,000 shares, about $2.285B (computed). That matches the Oppenheimer page title '$2.29 Billion Follow-On', so the baseline's $47 is correct but is not 'the' follow-on. #3 priced Jul 1, 2026 at $49.00, closed Jul 6, 2026: 14,555,925 company + 29,094,075 sellers = 43.65M shares, about $2.14B (computed). (4) Oppenheimer was a passive bookrunner on the IPO. The joint lead book-running managers were Goldman Sachs, Jefferies and Morgan Stanley. (5) The audit is also right that the baseline lacks operating data, and the filings supply much of it. FY ends June 30. FY2025 revenue was $753.2M (+56% YoY), with cost of revenues $475.1M and gross profit $278.1M, a computed GM of 36.9%. FY2026 revenue was $1,420.1M per the 10-K comparative table, consistent with 9M $958.4M + Q4 $462M. Q4 FY26 revenue was $462M (+94% YoY), adjusted EBITDA $113M (24.4% margin), and bookings $1,503M. Backlog: $849.9M at 6/30/25; $1,027.1M at 9/30/25 (~47% data center, 30% grid, 13% industrial, 10% other; ~37% from new customers); about $1.5B at 12/31/25; $1.98B at 3/31/26; $3.0B at 6/30/26 (+256% YoY). Customer concentration: no customer above 9% of FY2025 revenue, but one customer was about 12% of revenue in each of the quarters ended 12/31/25 and 3/31/26 (no customer above 10% over 9M FY26). Product mix: 'no product category represented more than 13% of revenues' in FY2025. The product list includes dry-type and liquid-filled transformers, switchboards, switchgear, PDUs, E-houses, ATS and others. Transformer revenue share, plant utilization and unit capacity are NOT disclosed in what I could retrieve, so the S-1 is only a partial source of transformer unit economics. The FY2026 full-year gross margin and FY2027 guidance were not retrieved.

result.analysis:
This run produced no new primary filing data. The workflow's shared web-search budget (200 searches per turn, across all agents) was already used up when this agent made its first query, and the egress policy blocks direct EDGAR, SEDAR+ and DART fetches. As instructed, I did not try to work around this. What follows is an audit of the company-filing evidence already in the baseline, plus a ranked plan for the next run. If more searching is needed, the user can send a follow-up message to start a turn with a fresh budget, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION.

What the audit means for a would-be transformer builder:

1. **The baseline is thin on the figures that matter most for entry economics.** For a builder, the key numbers are margins, utilization, price and mix, and customer concentration. The baseline has almost none of them.
   - It holds headline backlogs: GEV Electrification ~$41B, Quanta $53.4B, Eaton book-to-bill 1.3x, Hammond +96.9% YoY.
   - None of these is transformer-specific except GEV's ~$800M of US transformer orders.
   - The most useful missing document is Forgent's S-1/424B4 (audit-forgent-ipo-secondary). Forgent is the only recently listed pure-play North American distribution and data-center transformer maker. Its MD&A, risk factors and customer-concentration disclosures are the closest public stand-in for what a new entrant's P&L and customer risk would look like.

2. **The exit comparable needs a closer look.** The '~$10.5B Prolec GE' figure is a simple doubling of the $5.254B paid for half the company (audit-prolec-implied-value). That price bought control, so it may include a premium. The purchase-price allocation note in GEV's Q2 10-Q gives a better basis for valuation and should be read before the build-to-sell case leans on it.

3. **Several confidence tags are too generous.** These figures shape how competitors and demand are read, so they need primary checks before they drive any decision:
   - Hammond's figures are tagged [P] but come from trade press (audit-hammond-source-tag).
   - The Siemens Energy €51B backlog comes from a blog (audit-siemens-grid-backlog-source).
   - HD Hyundai's $8.5B backlog and 25.7% share come from an aggregator (audit-hdh-backlog-source).
   - The '>80% imported' LPT figure is cited to a news site (audit-lpt-import-share-tag).
   - The Korean 'about 25%' vs '25.7%' share figures cover different scopes (audit-korea-share-scope).
   - LS Electric's $123M order has no link at all (audit-ls-electric-no-url).

4. **Priority for the next run.** Ranked by value to an entrant:
   1. Forgent S-1 and 10-Q.
   2. Cleveland-Cliffs 10-Q (GOES pricing and volumes, Weirton status), because core steel is the gating input.
   3. GEV 10-Q (Electrification margin, Prolec allocation, capacity capex).
   4. Korean DART contracts. These give contract value per order and delivery windows, which show how far out EHV slots are booked.
   5. Hubbell and Eaton price contribution, to test whether the BLS index slowdown (+8.7% YoY) shows up in sellers' realized prices.
   6. The Worthington 10-K for third-party core capacity in Ontario and Mexico.

The baseline thesis is still plausible: strong demand, a timing risk from the 2027-29 capacity wave, and core steel as the binding constraint. Nothing in this domain confirmed or refuted it this run.

My search (allowed_domains woodmac.com: '... deficit 15% power transformers 8% substation $22 billion') returned 'web search budget is used up'. WebFetch/curl are blocked. Local check found two sourcing defects in the finding's detail. (1) 'The 2025 figures come from POWER magazine' is documented only for the 30% power figure: indicators.csv row 10 links https://www.powermag.com/transformers-in-2026-shortage-scramble-or-self-inflicted-crisis/, and build_data.py line 74 labels it 'Wood Mackenzie Q2 2025 survey'. The 2025 substation figure of 10% has no row or URL in indicators.csv, build_data.py or the weekly report. It appears only in market-map.md line 16 ('was 30% / 10% in 2025'), tagged WoodMac [S] with no link. (2) The '2026 down from 2025' comparison joins two different WoodMac publications: a Q2 2025 survey reported by POWER, and a Sep 2026 EO 14420 release (build_data.py line 75). Unless the EO release states both years itself, part of the halving from 30% to 15% may reflect a change in method rather than supply catching up. The 2026 figures (15% power, 8% substation) are consistent across indicators.csv rows 8-9 and build_data.py line 26, all citing the WoodMac EO URL. That is one source repeated, not corroboration. The ~5% by 2030 projection is correctly flagged W (DistroForge, build_data.py line 76). The weekly report (line 58) and dashboard (line 203) lean on 'gap fell from 30% to 15% in a year' as a timing-risk argument, so the comparability issue matters for the entry decision.

findings.claim: Carried from the baseline, not re-verified this run: Wood Mackenzie says more than $22B of bulk-power equipment imports since 2025 are exposed to EO 14420, and the 100 MVA+ segment is hit hardest.
findings.detail: This matters for demand facing domestic and allied suppliers. If DOE's ~Dec 24, 2026 rules cover data-center substations, demand that Chinese imports were meeting moves to non-covered suppliers. This shifts demand between suppliers; it does not add to total demand.
findings.verify_evidence: No independent check was possible: the search budget was exhausted and WebFetch/curl are blocked. Every baseline instance cites the same single WoodMac URL: market-map.md line 156, weekly line 34, indicators.csv row 20 and build_data.py line 49. The trade_flows researcher in this run produced the same finding from the same URL ('almost all from China'), which matches build_data.py's wording 'nearly all from China'. That points to a baseline carry-over, not an independent read. Three issues. (1) The as-of date is inconsistent: the finding says 2026-08, build_data.py says 2026-09, and indicators.csv says '2025-2026'. The baseline dates the EO Aug 26, 2026, so the release is on or after that date; the exact day is unconfirmed. Treat it as '2026-08/09'. (2) The EO number is disputed inside the baseline: market-map uses 14420 and notes it is 'cited as 14421 by some firms', and the McGuireWoods URL slug in the weekly report says 14421. Check the Federal Register before citing it. (3) There is a substantive tension with this run's trade data. trade_flows (Census-derived via a NextMSC vendor report, W) puts total 2025 imports of >100 MVA liquid transformers at $2.77B, with China about 2% of units. Computed: $22B / $2.77B = about 7.9x. So most of the >$22B must be inverters, BESS, breakers or sub-100 MVA transformers, not 100 MVA+ units. 'The 100 MVA+ segment is hit hardest' can hold only if WoodMac means the resulting shortage in that segment, not China's import share in it. The finding's conclusion, that this shifts demand between suppliers and does not add to total demand, is sound reasoning and does not depend on the number.

result.analysis:
This run produced no new primary data. All three opening WebSearch calls (PUCT/ERCOT 765 kV approvals, STEP autotransformer counts, ERCOT large-load queue) were refused. The 200-search-per-turn budget shared by this workflow's agents was already used up, and the egress policy blocks WebFetch and curl. As instructed, I did not work around either limit. The findings only restate baseline datapoints that have URLs, so the demand anchors sit in one table, plus one data-quality finding. None of it should be read as newly verified.

What the existing sourced evidence supports. The spending envelope is large and still rising: EEI projects $239B for 2026 and $1.4T for 2026-30 (eei-capex-2026), and RRA projects $1.295T (rra-capex-2026-30). Order books at the companies that sell into it are at records: GE Vernova Electrification ~$41B (gev-electrification-backlog), Eaton book-to-bill 1.3 (eaton-btb), Quanta $53.4B (quanta-backlog). Hyperscalers now buy 765/345 kV units directly (hyosung-dc-765). EO 14420 moves >$22B of import-served demand toward non-Chinese suppliers (woodmac-eo-exposure). Against this, WoodMac's deficit halves from 30% to 15% between 2025 and 2026 (woodmac-deficit). Supply is responding faster than demand is growing in aggregate. The baseline's ~5% gap by 2030 comes from a weak source.

What it does not yet support. The key question for an entrant is whether 2027-29 demand outpaces the 2027-29 capacity wave, and nothing quantified from this run answers it. Every input that would size unit demand is missing: autotransformer counts in ERCOT STEP, PJM, MISO Tranche 2.1 and SPP; GSU demand implied by turbine GW and EIA additions; large-load GW; NREL distribution stock growth. Six baseline demand claims the bull case leans on have no URL (baseline-unsourced-demand): the $9.4B Eastern Backbone, ~$36B STEP, the Hillje three-unit spec, the Transource award, GE Vernova's $2.7B of data-center orders and its >100 GW gas backlog. They need sourcing before any capital decision.

Method for the follow-up run (no numbers assumed). For EHV, read the substation scope in each approved CCN or RTEP project, count units (single-phase banks x 3 plus spares, or three-phase units), assign each to its in-service year and shift 3-4 years earlier for order timing. For GSUs, convert turbine-backlog GW and EIA-860M planned units into units per plant. Then compare annual units with the unit rates in capacity_expansions.csv: Hyosung 250+/yr, Prolec Goldsboro 420/yr, Siemens Charlotte 57 LPT/yr, HD Hyundai +50% EHV.

Provisional view, low confidence and not newly evidenced. Aggregate power-transformer tightness is easing. The segments with the most concentrated, dated demand, 765 kV autotransformers and GSUs, have the fewest qualified suppliers, so they are the most likely to stay short through 2029. The 765 kV class remains a poor fit for a new entrant because of capital and qualification. Re-run with fresh search budget to test this; the gaps list gives a domain-targeted query plan for each missing item.

result.analysis:
This run found no new primary data. All five searches in the first batch returned "web search budget used up": the 200-call limit is shared by every agent in this workflow turn and was already exhausted. Covered: Hitachi Varennes, Delta Star Saint-Jean, Hydro-Québec framework agreements, Prolec GE Apodaca, and Chinese makers in Mexico. As the tool instructed, I did not work around the limit. What follows is (a) baseline data re-tabulated for this domain and marked not re-verified, and (b) a local check of how well the baseline's sources hold up. To continue, the user can send a follow-up message or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION. The "Follow-up search plan" table has ~23 targeted queries ready to run.

**What the baseline already says.** Canada and Mexico are mostly incumbent territory. Only three projects have dollar figures:
- Hitachi Varennes: C$270M + C$140M, ~3x capacity, test bay by end-2027. The USD conversion and whether the two amounts add up are unclear (baseline-varennes-fx).
- Prolec GE Monterrey: US$85M, completion not confirmed.
- WEG Atotonilco de Tula: US$156M, completion not confirmed.

Hammond's Mexican dry-type plant is operating, but its only source is trade press (baseline-tag-hammond-mx). Mexico's place as the largest US import source by value (~$2.3B, 2023) traces to an aggregator and should be treated as weak (baseline-tag-mexico-imports). That figure is the key input for sizing nearshore competition, and it is three years old.

**Unknowns that matter for a builder, in priority order:**
1. **Chinese-linked capacity inside USMCA.** The list could not be verified. The only lead with a direct US tie is JST Power Equipment (Wytheville VA, pad-mount, 1,000 units/yr from 2027), which the baseline lists as private. From unverified background knowledge, it may belong to China's Jinpan. If so, it contradicts the baseline and is the clearest test case for EO 14420.
2. **Who counts as a covered entity.** The 2020 bulk-power order (EO 13920) used an "owned, controlled, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of a foreign adversary" test; this is background and needs checking against EO 14420. If DOE's December rules copy it, Chinese-owned plants in Mexico or the US would be caught regardless of where they are. That helps non-Chinese entrants.
3. **Cost of a Mexican-built unit.** This turns on three things: the USMCA rule of origin for HTS 8504 when cores or GOES are imported, how Section 232 and 301 treat USMCA-qualifying units, and Mexico's 2026 tariff increases on Asian inputs.
4. **Canadian demand and trade policy.** Hydro-Québec, Hydro One and BC Hydro buying, plus Canada's steel countermeasures, decide whether a Canadian plant serves protected local demand or exports.

**Implication:** until items 1 to 3 are filled, treat Mexico as a competitive threat of unknown size and Canada as a market dominated by incumbents. Do not choose a plant location based on this domain's output.

result.analysis:
This run produced no new primary data. The 200-search WebSearch budget, shared by every agent in this turn, was already used up when this agent made its first four queries (Virginia Transformer sale, JST ownership, Giga Energy funding, MacLean–Delta Star price). All four were refused, and the harness said not to work around the limit. Direct fetches to government and filing sites are blocked by egress policy. Everything below comes from the local baseline, and none of it was independently re-checked. To continue, the user can send a follow-up message after this reply, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION. The priority queue table lists the exact primary sources to query next.

What the baseline already supports for someone thinking about building transformers:
1. Exit valuations are high. GE Vernova paid $5.254B for half of Prolec GE, implying about $10.5B for 100% (prolec_implied_100pct). Blackstone reportedly paid about $4B for MacLean and is now using it to buy Delta Star (maclean_lbo_4b). Forgent's follow-on priced 74% above its IPO (forgent_reprice_74pct). Virginia Transformer tested a sale above $6B (vtc_sale_talk_6b). This supports a build-to-sell plan.
2. None of these has a multiple. No revenue or EBITDA was obtained for Prolec, MacLean, Delta Star, Virginia Transformer or Forgent. Until the GE Vernova Prolec disclosures and Forgent's S-1 and 10-Qs are pulled, any EV/EBITDA figure would be a guess. Virginia Transformer has gone more than 18 months without a deal at the reported >$6B, which hints that bids may have come in below the ask. That is an inference only.
3. JST's ownership is the most decision-relevant open item (jst_profile_owner_unverified). If JST is controlled from a foreign-adversary country, DOE's EO 14420 rules (~Dec 24, 2026) could take about 1,000 pad-mount units a year out of the domestic-competitor set. Check the Virginia SCC entity record and the original VEDP or governor announcement first.
4. Private-equity money keeps going into refurbishment, mobile and rental assets (delta_star_profile, sunbelt_tjc_unconfirmed). Venture money is going into new medium-voltage and solid-state makers (giga_houston_conflict; Heron, DG Matrix and Amperesand in the table). A new entrant will meet both kinds of capital as buyers and as competitors.
5. The Indian entry route (marsons_cleanhill_jv) starts with imports, not US manufacturing. That points to import price competition rather than more US capacity in the near term. Turkish, Vietnamese, Brazilian and European entrants could not be assessed this run.

Every row in the tables is labeled carried-forward, and every multiple cell is blank on purpose. The next run should start with the priority queue rather than broad news searches.

result.analysis:
Bottom line for this domain: I could not run any new primary research. The 200-search limit per turn, shared by every agent in the workflow, was already used up before my first query. As instructed, I did not work around it with curl, proxies or archives. Every finding here is restated from the 2026-10-11 baseline and was not re-verified. To fill the domain, the user can send a follow-up message to start a fresh run with a new search budget, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION. The gaps list is written so that run can work through it query by query.

What the baseline already supports for someone building transformers:
- **GOES is the clearest bottleneck.** Cleveland-Cliffs is the only US producer, and its expansion is incremental: $200M plus a $75M DOE award for up to +25% output, with no date or tonnage disclosed (baseline-goes-butler-expansion). Its ~920mm width and higher-loss grades leave large-power-transformer core makers on imports (baseline-goes-sole-domestic-width). Prices roughly doubled from 2020 to 2024 (baseline-goes-price-doubled).
- **Federal funding is a possible route.** DPA PD 2026-10 explicitly covers electrical core steel (baseline-dpa-core-steel), so DOE Title III money could back an upstream or core-cutting entrant.
- **Incumbents are locking up components.** Hitachi is buying Canduct (insulation kits, baseline-hitachi-canduct) and building a captive bushings plant (baseline-hitachi-alamo-bushings), so a new builder may find fewer kits and bushings sold on the open market.
- **Conductor cost risk is high.** Section 232 tiers apply to copper (baseline-copper-232), and copper is near its record (baseline-copper-price). Whether magnet wire falls in the 50% tier is unresolved.

**One baseline correction is needed.** The dashboard shows a 50% tariff on imported cores and laminations, sourced to an x.com post. That conflicts with the Apr 2026 tiered regime described in market-map.md, which is the better source (baseline-s232-cores-rate-conflict). Confirm the rate against the Proclamation 11021 annex before modelling imported-core costs.

**Not covered at all yet:**
- GOES import volumes by country and current GOES prices.
- Foreign GOES makers' US plans.
- Metglas amorphous capacity and how the DOE 2029 rule would shift core demand toward amorphous (baseline-doe-efficiency-rule).
- Magnet-wire, oil/ester and OLTC capacity.
- Measured lead times for any component.

The bottleneck ranking table is therefore a provisional judgment, not sourced data. The practical advice for a new builder doesn't change: secure core supply (Cliffs allocation, imported GOES priced at the correct 232 tier, or a contracted core maker such as Worthington Burlington) and test-bay access before committing to a site.

findings.claim: Computed from baseline data: only four North American power-transformer expansions state capacity in units per year, and together they add roughly 394-427 units/yr by about 2028.
findings.entity: Siemens Energy Charlotte; Prolec GE Goldsboro; Hyosung HICO Memphis; Niagara Power Transformer
findings.detail: Computed by summing baseline inputs. None was re-verified this run because the search budget was used up. Siemens Charlotte '24 -> 57 LPT/yr' (investing.com, https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/siemens-energy-targets-us-transformer-production-in-2027-can-further-expand-factory-4113341). The plant is new with no existing US output, so the increment is 24 in phase 1 and up to 57 if the expansion option is exercised. Goldsboro 220 -> 420 (+200, end-2027). Hyosung Memphis 130 -> 250+ (+120, 2027-28; https://evertiq.com/news/2026-09-18-hyosung-secures-287-million-us-orders-for-uhv-transformers). Niagara 90 -> 140 (+50, online date not stated; https://www.ien.com/operations/news/22973547/centuryold-transformer-maker-plans-71m-expansion-in-new-york). Sum: 24+200+120+50 = 394, or 427 with Siemens at 57. The three operating plants go from 440 to 810 units/yr. Size classes are mixed: Goldsboro and Niagara build medium as well as large power, so this is not a >100 MVA figure. No source gives MVA/yr.

findings.claim: Computed: if the unverified count of 2,268 imported >100 MVA units in 2025 is right, the stated LPT/EHV additions (Siemens Charlotte plus Hyosung Memphis, 144-177 units/yr) would replace only about 6-8% of 2025 import volume, or 5-6% of the 2,901-unit trailing-12-month count to Jun-2026.
findings.detail:
Numerator (baseline, S): Siemens +24 to +57; Hyosung +120. Sum 144-177.
Denominators: 2,268 (2025) and 2,901 (TTM Jun-2026). These come from nextmsc as relayed by the task brief. The exact page URL is not in the baseline files, the figures were not verified this run, and the primary HTS 8504.23.0080 Census/USITC series was not reached.

Ratios:
- LPT/EHV adds: 144/2,268 = 6.3%; 177/2,268 = 7.8%; 144/2,901 = 5.0%; 177/2,901 = 6.1%.
- All four stated plants (394-427): 17.4-18.8% of 2025 imports; 13.6-14.7% of TTM.

The all-plant ratio overstates the LPT case because Goldsboro and Niagara units are partly <100 MVA. Even taken at face value, stated domestic LPT additions are small against the import pool, so there is no sign of an LPT glut from domestic additions alone in 2028.

findings.claim: Computed cross-check: Siemens Energy's statement that more than 80% of US LPT demand is imported, combined with 2,268 >100 MVA imports, implies US >100 MVA output of at most about 567 units/yr. Yet three existing plants alone list 440 units/yr, so unit counts from different sources are not on the same size basis.
findings.detail:
Computed:
- Total = 2,268 / 0.80 = 2,835. Domestic = 2,835 - 2,268 = 567. This is an upper bound, because the import share is '>80%'.
- Existing stated capacity: Goldsboro 220 + Hyosung 130 + Niagara 90 = 440 units/yr.
- That 440 excludes Hitachi South Boston, PTT Canonsburg, Mitsubishi Memphis, HD Hyundai Montgomery, VTC, Delta Star, Howard and WEG Washington MO.

At least one of these must hold:
(a) most Goldsboro and Niagara units are <100 MVA;
(b) Siemens' 'LPT' definition differs from >100 MVA;
(c) the nextmsc import count is wrong.

Implication: ratios by segment must be built in MVA, or in units within a strict size band, not by mixing unit counts across sources.

findings.claim: Wood Mackenzie puts the US power-transformer supply deficit at 30% in 2025 and 15% in 2026, and the substation-unit deficit at 10% and 8%. Supply therefore covered about 85% of power-transformer demand and 92% of substation demand in 2026.
findings.detail: The 2025 power figure comes via POWER magazine (https://www.powermag.com/transformers-in-2026-shortage-scramble-or-self-inflicted-crisis/). gap_fill.analysis:
This run added no new primary evidence. The shared per-turn WebSearch cap (200 calls across all agents) was used up before this agent's first query returned, and direct fetches are blocked. Everything here is rearranged and computed from the baseline, and each computed ratio is only as reliable as its weakest input. The deliverable asked for (2028 capacity divided by 2028 demand for each segment) cannot be computed honestly for any segment: none has both a stated NA capacity base and a unit or MVA demand forecast.

What the baseline does support:

1) Disclosure is poorest where the money is. Only four power plants state units/yr; together they add about 394-427 units/yr by around 2028 (supply-power-stated-adds). The other 12, including Hitachi South Boston, Hitachi Gallman, VTC Muscle Shoals and HD Hyundai #2, give only percentage uplifts, floor space, jobs or dollars (supply-power-unstated). Any announced-MVA total will be a floor.

2) At the top end, the import pool dwarfs stated domestic additions. If the unverified 2,268-unit >100 MVA import count is right, stated LPT/EHV additions (Siemens plus Hyosung) would replace only about 6-8% of 2025 imports, and under 20% even counting all four plants (import-substitution-ratio). On current evidence, LPT/EHV and GSU are not at glut risk in 2028, and GSU remains the tightest class by lead time (leadtime-ladder, gsu-demand-proxy).

3) The denominators do not reconcile. Siemens' figure of more than 80% imported, applied to 2,268 imports, caps US >100 MVA output at about 567 units, yet three existing plants list 440 units/yr (lpt-denominator-inconsistency). Unit counts from different sources mix size classes, so the segment build has to be done in MVA.

4) The ~5% deficit for 2030 is still sourced only to a vendor blog [W] (deficit-2030-unverified). WoodMac's own Sep 2026 release says EO 14420 will worsen the shortage, with 100 MVA+ hit hardest (eo-worsens-deficit). Treat 5% as an optimistic, probably pre-EO path; the 2026 figures (15% power, 8% substation) are the last solid reading (deficit-2025-2026).

5) Glut risk, if it comes, shows first in distribution and medium power. Distribution and dry-type show the first loosening: Hammond's backlog fell 6.9% QoQ and price growth is slowing (distribution-easing-signals), although Eaton's book-to-bill is still 1.3 (eaton-demand-signal). The largest new 3-phase plants (Eaton, ERMCO) state no unit capacity. Medium power (10-160 MVA) is where Gallman, Muscle Shoals, Goldsboro, Howard and Rincon all open in 2027-29, the same window as a new entrant.

For a builder, the lean is unchanged but not yet proven: plan around GSU and large power staying import-dependent through 2028, and expect medium power and pad-mount to tighten least, or loosen. Also note the brief's 4,400-jobs figure is 3,189 in the baseline CSV (jobs-2027-28-reconcile). Re-run this domain once search budget is available.

findings.claim: No US government price series separates distribution transformers from power transformers any more. BLS's distribution-transformer industry product index (PCU3353113353111) ended in Feb 2023, leaving only the blended WPU117409 (power and distribution) and WPU117411 (other and parts).
findings.detail: From sibling findings bls-detail-cuts and ppi-history-dec. PCU3353113353111: 197.30 (Dec 2019), 315.71 (Dec 2022), 333.1 (Feb 2023), then discontinued (FRED date range). BLS dropped about 350 more PPIs from Jan 2026 data, and it is unconfirmed whether other transformer series were among them. Implication: any 'distribution softening vs power' test must come from procurement records, Census unit values by HTS 8504.21/.22/.23, or maker disclosures. Official indexes cannot answer it.

findings.claim: The blended power-and-distribution PPI (WPU117409) jumped 4.6% in a single step in Jul 2026 to a record 381.783, +8.7% YoY, after a flat Q2. Prices moved in discrete resets, not monthly drift.
findings.detail: Staircase: 351.192 (Jul-Sep 2025), 362.638 (Jan-Mar 2026), 364.861 (Apr-Jun 2026), 381.783 (Jul 2026). Computed: 381.783/351.192 = +8.71% YoY; 381.783/364.861 = +4.64% MoM. The NAICS 335311 industry PPI was 475.065 in Aug 2026, +7.8% YoY (computed 475.065/440.550). The baseline calls prices 'still rising, decelerating', which these vintages contradict. Because the index blends segments, a distribution price decline could be hidden by faster power-price growth, but a record print with a +4.6% step is hard to square with a broad distribution price war. Same data as sibling ppi-wpu117409-jul26 and ppi-momentum-reaccel. Not re-verified. Sep data due Oct 15, 2026.

findings.claim: The only recent decline in transformer PPIs was small and brief. NAICS 335311 slipped 0.9% from its Oct 2025 peak (458.356) to Apr 2026 (454.338), and WPU1174 fell 1.5% from Feb to Apr 2026, before July's jump.
findings.detail: Computed: 454.338/458.356 = -0.88%; WPU1174 415.235/421.523 = -1.49%. WPU117411 (other transformers and parts) fell 5.0% from 247.039 (Jan-Mar 2026) to 234.725 (Apr 2026), then rose to 240.545 in May. My inference: this soft patch overlaps the period of the softening anecdotes (Hammond's Canadian pricing in Q2'26). That fits a mild, short-lived softening that ended with the July reset, not a sustained price war. From sibling ppi-335311-softpatch.

findings.claim: Korea's pole-mount transformer exports (oil-immersed, ≤100 kV) averaged only about $18M in Q2 2025, down more than half year on year, as small Korean makers lost US orders.
findings.unit: USD m (Q2 2025 average; monthly vs quarterly basis ambiguous)
findings.detail: Causes cited: more US supply sources, tariff risk, and quality problems (overweight units, design defects) that pushed buyers to Latin American suppliers. Read: US buyers switch freely among imported distribution suppliers, which signals competition. But the cited cause is partly quality, not price, so this is not proof of falling prices. Contrast: Korea's >10 MVA exports to the US rose 83% in 2025 (sibling korea-us-uhv-2023-2025). From sibling korea-pole-transformers. Not re-verified.

findings.claim: CRS (Apr 23, 2026) reports that the US imports about 25-30% of its distribution transformers, mainly from Taiwan, Canada and Mexico, and that BLS data show distribution and large power transformer prices up about 40% in real terms from 2020 to 2024.
findings.detail: CRS also notes DOE found transformer prices tracking GOES prices from 2021, and that imported electrical-steel articles have faced 50% tariffs since Aug 15, 2025. Policy options it lists include extending 45X to distribution transformers (S.448/H.R.4128). Implication: distribution import competition comes from allied and nearshore suppliers, so EO 14420 will not remove it. A 45X extension would be a material margin lever for a distribution builder. From sibling goes-crs. Not re-verified.

findings.claim: Section 232 treats the segments differently: extra-high-voltage transformers carry a temporary 15% rate through Dec 31, 2027 (Annex III), while distribution transformers stay at 25% (Annex I-B).
findings.detail: Proclamation 11032 (91 FR 34085, effective Jun 8, 2026) expanded the 15% tier. The Annex III extraction was garbled. This confirms the baseline's narrow reading. Implication: a US builder gets more tariff shelter in distribution than in LPT, which is also where Indian, Mexican and Canadian suppliers are pushing hardest. From sibling sec232-transformer-tiers.

findings.claim: India-built, US-designed suppliers advertise short lead times. Zetwerk claims more than 1,000 MVA a month of capacity and 12-24 week lead times. Ayr Energy reported more than $500M of contracts by Apr 2026 and publishes 40-72 week power-transformer lead times.

If 12-24 weeks holds for distribution classes, it beats the baseline's 26-60 week domestic range by 2-3x, which is a price-pressure channel. findings.claim: Korea's US-bound ultra-high-voltage transformer export price rose 20.2% to $22,920/ton in 2025 (from $19,060), 17.5% above Korea's world average of $19,495/ton.
findings.detail: KITA data via Herald Economy. Computed: 22,920/19,060 = +20.2%; 22,920/19,495 = +17.6% (17.5% as reported). The article's US tonnage has a unit error, so only $/t is used. This is the cleanest power-segment price proxy found: imported EHV prices rose about 20% in one year, while the blended PPI's 2025 annual average rose only about 3% (NextMSC, W). findings.claim: Korean >10 MVA export prices kept rising in 2026 but more slowly. Jan-Jul 2026 exports of $822.32M for 39,747 tons imply about $20,689/ton, +6.1% on the 2025 world average of $19,495/ton. US-bound value ran 38% above its 2025 monthly pace.
findings.detail: Computed: $822.32M / 39,747 t = $20,689/t, and 20,689/19,495 = +6.1%. The article prints $26,890/t (+6.2%). That level does not reconcile with value over tonnage, but its +6.2% matches the computed growth, so the printed level is probably a typo. US-bound Jan-Jul 2026 was $595.58M, or $85.1M a month vs $61.5M in 2025 (+38%, computed), and the US took 72% of the total. A 2026 US-only $/t cannot be computed because the tonnage is misreported. Read: power-segment import prices are still rising in 2026 but slowing from about +20% to about +6% on a world basis, so power is decelerating too, not only distribution. Built from sibling korea-global-uhv-2026 and korea-us-uhv-2026-janjul.

findings.claim: US imports of >100 MVA liquid transformers rose from 617 units ($0.62B) in 2019 to 2,268 units ($2.77B) in 2025, and to 2,901 units in the 12 months to Jun 2026 (+27.9% on 2025).
findings.detail: Census-derived, via a vendor report. Computed implied unit value: $1.005M (2019) to $1.221M (2025), +21.5%. That is far below the PPI's roughly +91% and implausibly low for >100 MVA units, so the sibling verifier flagged a scope or unit-count problem (for example, disassembled shipments). Do NOT use it as a $/MVA price. As a volume signal, imported LPT demand is still growing about 28%. From sibling lpt-100mva-2025 and lpt-100mva-ttm-2026.

gap_fill.analysis:
Bottom line: this run could not test the hypothesis directly. All four searches were refused because the workflow's shared budget of 200 searches per turn was already used up (run-status-blocked). So the core deliverables are missing: 0 of the 25 buyer-level award datapoints, no $/kVA or $/MVA series, and no maker margins for Forgent, Hammond, HD Hyundai, Hyosung or Hubbell. What follows re-assembles segment-relevant evidence that sibling domains gathered earlier in this workflow. It is not independent confirmation. To continue, the user can send a follow-up message (a new turn has a fresh search budget) or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION. Table 4 is a ready query plan.

The segment split cannot come from official data: BLS stopped publishing a distribution-only index in Feb 2023 (seg-no-official-split). Bid tabs, Census HS 8504.21/.22/.23 unit values and maker filings are the only routes.

Distribution. The case for softening rests on import-channel signals, not on prices:
- Korean pole-mount exports more than halved, partly over quality problems (seg-dist-korea-pole).
- India-built suppliers claim 12-24 week lead times (seg-india-leadtimes, W) and are now suing each other at the USITC (seg-india-337).
- Hammond's dry-type backlog fell 6.9% quarter on quarter, with softer Canadian pricing (seg-hammond-soft).

Against that:
- The blended producer price index (PPI) hit a record after a +4.6% step in July (seg-ppi-blended-reaccel). Its only dip was a 0.9-1.5% soft patch from Q4'25 to Q2'26 (seg-ppi-softpatch).
- Industry capacity utilization is about 86% (seg-capacity-util).
- Eaton's book-to-bill is 1.3 (seg-eaton-btb).
- WoodMac still shows an 8% deficit for smaller units (seg-woodmac-deficit-split).

The baseline's "lead times easing" call has no primary support (seg-dist-leadtime-audit).

Power and LPT. Prices are still rising but slowing. Korean US-bound prices per ton rose 20% in 2025, and the world-basis price is up about 6% in Jan-Jul 2026 (seg-power-korea-price, seg-power-korea-2026). Units of >100 MVA imports are up 28% (seg-power-lpt-imports). WoodMac's power deficit halved from 30% to 15%, a faster close than the smaller-unit deficit.

Verdict: not established. I found no evidence that distribution transaction prices are falling. There are signs that the imported, commodity end of distribution (single-phase pole-mount) has become contestable, and that price growth is slowing in power as well. "A distribution price war while LPT keeps scarcity margins" remains a hypothesis.

For a builder:
1. Do not underwrite distribution at today's prices beyond 2027. Distribution has more tariff shelter than LPT (25% vs 15% plus 0-4.32% antidumping; seg-tariff-split, seg-korea-ad). But allied and nearshore imports, mainly Taiwan, Canada and Mexico (seg-dist-crs), plus India-built entrants contest it. Cheaper aluminum gives aluminum-wound distribution makers room to cut prices without losing margin (seg-al-cu-cost). Oil and copper costs push the other way (seg-oil-cost).
2. Power pricing has more momentum, but its deficit is closing fastest, and Korean rivals face near-zero antidumping duty.
3. The decisive missing data are utility bid tabs (weeks ARO and $/unit for 25/50 kVA pole-mount and 75-2,500 kVA pad-mount) and Forgent's and Hammond's gross margins. Q3 reports in late Oct and Nov are the next read.

findings.entity: EO 13920 (2020), predecessor with the identical title
findings.claim: EO 13920 (May 1, 2020), titled 'Securing the United States Bulk-Power System', defined the bulk-power system to include transmission lines rated 69 kV or more and to exclude 'facilities used in the local distribution of electric energy'. Its covered equipment included substation transformers, instrument transformers, reactors, capacitors, high-voltage breakers, generation turbines and control systems.
findings.value: 69 kV and above; local distribution excluded
findings.detail: This is a primary document, but it is cited from model background knowledge (pre-June 2026). It was not retrieved in this run, and the URL and FR doc number are from memory, so verify both. If the 2026 order or DOE's December rules reuse this definition, three things follow. Pole and pad-mount distribution units serving loads, including most data-center MV pad-mounts at ≤34.5 kV, would fall outside scope. Data-center main substation transformers interconnected at 69 kV or more would fall inside. Utility-scale inverters and battery storage would come in through the clause on generation needed for transmission reliability. EO 13920 also let the Secretary pre-qualify equipment and vendors and directed work to identify, isolate, monitor or replace installed foreign-adversary equipment. Both points come from memory and need checking against the 2026 text.

findings.claim: EO 13920 reached equipment 'designed, developed, manufactured, or supplied by persons owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of a foreign adversary' in transactions started after the order date. That test follows the owner, not the factory location.
findings.detail: From model background knowledge, not retrieved here. The 2026 order's 'transactions after Aug 26' trigger (covered-equipment-headline) matches the 13920 structure. If the same test is used, Chinese-owned plants in Mexico or the US would be caught, and USMCA origin would not help. A possible example is JST Power Equipment, Wytheville VA, if it has a PRC parent; its ownership is unverified (see gaps). Confirm the test in the 2026 text and the RFI questions.

findings.detail: Computed: 0.022 × 2,268 = 49.9. This is a Census-derived vendor series collected by a sibling agent earlier in this session. A sibling verifier marked it 'unverifiable' and it was not re-checked here. Whatever the scope issue (nextmsc-scope-risk), fewer than 1% of WoodMac's >8,000 Chinese units can be ≥100 MVA units (50 / 8,000 = 0.6%, computed).

findings.claim: The '>100 MVA' import series behind the 2.2% figure may actually cover all >10 MVA (8504.23) units: its implied average is only $1.22M per unit, and its 2025 value is 44% above the whole of 8504.23 imports in 2023.
findings.detail: Computed: $2.77B / 2,268 = $1.221M per unit. $2.77B / $1.92B = 1.44. The 2023 8504.23 total of $1.92B comes from TrendEconomy (https://trendeconomy.com/data/h2/UnitedStatesOfAmerica/8504). The Mexico unit value of about $0.71M is far below typical LPT pricing. If the series really is all of 8504.23, China's ~50 units would be its entire >10 MVA count for 2025, which pushes the >8,000 even further below 10 MVA. A DataWeb pull of 8504.23.0040 and 8504.23.0080 by country would settle it.

The 'fewer than 1,500 in 2022' comparison reads most naturally as an annual rate, meaning more than 8,000 in Jan-Oct 2025. That is the main reading tested in reconcile-value-ceiling. WoodMac's definition was not found in this run.

findings.claim: China supplied about $3.6B, roughly 10%, of US HS 8504 imports in 2025, down from about 27% of the total in 2020. Comtrade mirrors give $4.0B for 2024 and $4.27B for 2023.
findings.detail: The 2024 and 2025 cross-checks come from Trading Economics (Comtrade mirror) and 2023 from TrendEconomy. HS 8504 is dominated by 8504.40 static converters and power supplies, which also hold inverters, so China's transformer-only value is well below $3.6B. Its split by HTS-10 line was not found.

findings.claim: If the >8,000 Chinese units arrived in Jan-Oct 2025, their average declared value could not exceed about $375k each even if every dollar of China's HS 8504 exports to the US were these transformers. That is below every per-unit value found for >10 MVA imports, so most of the units must sit below 10 MVA, in 8504.22 (liquid, 650 kVA-10 MVA) and/or 8504.34 (dry, >500 kVA).
findings.detail: Computed: $3.6B × 10/12 / 8,000 = $375k. This assumes an even monthly flow, and the real ceiling is lower because 8504.40 converters make up much of China's HS 8504. Per-unit values found for >10 MVA imports: about $0.71M (Mexico, W), about $1.22M (nextmsc average) and about $2.29M (Korea, $738.28M / 323 units). At $0.71M, 8,000 units would be worth $5.68B, more than China's entire HS 8504 shipments ($3.6B). Caveats: (1) no unit value specific to 10-100 MVA was found, so the test is strong but not conclusive for 8504.23.0040. (2) If the >8,000 is a cumulative 2022-Oct 2025 count, the ceiling rises to about $1.49M per unit ($11.9B from 2023-25 / 8,000, excluding 2022), and the test no longer constrains the answer.

findings.claim: All of China's HS 8504 shipments to the US, transformers plus inverters and converters, from Jan 2025 to Aug 2026 add up to at most about $7.1B, about a third of WoodMac's >$22B 'exposed' figure. Most of the exposed value must therefore be other equipment such as battery storage, not transformers.
findings.detail: Computed: $3.6B (2025, CPA) + $3.6B × 1.45 × 8/12 (2026 Jan-Aug, using the W-grade +45% H1-2026 US-bound growth from ksher) = $7.08B. $7.08B / $22B = 32%. So the displaced Chinese transformer business is at most single-digit billions of dollars a year, not $22B. Size a factory against the transformer HTS lines.

findings.entity: China share of US transformer and switchgear supply
findings.claim: WoodMac's Boucher told CNBC on Sep 3, 2026 that China's share approaches 30% only in 'certain' transformer and switchgear categories, while Goldman puts China at about 4% of the US transformer market overall.
findings.detail: The Goldman ~4% figure has no URL in the sibling notes. Read together with the ~2% share at ≥100 MVA (china-share-gt100mva), the 30% categories are most likely data-center MV pad-mount, dry-type and unit-substation transformers and switchgear. That is an inference.

findings.entity: China >10 MVA exports to the US, 2026
findings.claim: Goldman (Mar 26, 2026, via Sina) reported that China's >10 MVA transformer exports reached RMB4.4B in Jan-Feb 2026 (+61%), that US-bound shipments grew 182% with units mostly in the 10-220 MVA range, and that US-bound growth then slowed to +118% in March and +95% in April.
findings.detail: This shows the China mix moving up into 8504.23.0040 (10-100 MVA) in 2026, after WoodMac's Oct 2025 window. The growth rates may be off a small base, and absolute US-bound units and values were not found. The 10-100 MVA flow is the one most clearly covered by a 69 kV-plus BPS definition.

findings.entity: China liquid-dielectric transformers to North America
findings.claim: China's liquid-dielectric transformer exports fell 2.6% year on year to RMB4.212B in August 2026. North America-bound shipments were up 111% year on year but down 35.7% from July. Jan-Aug liquid exports totaled RMB33.294B (+25.07%).
findings.detail: Changjiang Securities, citing GACC. August mostly predates the Aug 26 EO, so the month-on-month drop may reflect pre-EO caution or lumpy shipments. September is the first clean post-EO month.

findings.claim: China's transformer exports totaled $7.95B in Jan-Aug 2026 (+28.5%). August was $1.067B (+14.8%), the slowest growth this year, and the US was the largest single destination.
findings.detail: Caixin Securities, citing GACC. US-bound absolute values by HS line (85042200, 85042300, 85043400) for 2026 were not found.

findings.claim: China exported a record RMB64.6B of transformers in 2025 at an average of RMB205,000 per unit, which implies about 315,000 units shipped worldwide. WoodMac's >8,000 US units would be about 2.5% of that.
findings.detail: Computed: 64.6e9 / 205,000 = 315,122 units, and 8,000 / 315,122 = 2.5%. The average of RMB205k (about $28-29k) shows that China's export count is dominated by small and medium units.

findings.claim: US HS 8504 imports from Vietnam were $1.66B in 2024, while China's HS 8504 exports to Vietnam doubled from $1.5B to $3.0B over 2020-2025. Thailand supplied $3.3B of US HS 8504 imports in 2025, mostly power supplies and converters.
findings.detail: CPA calls the Vietnam pattern a transshipment signal, not confirmed evasion. No transformer-specific HTS-10 data for Vietnam or Thailand was found. Under an ownership-based entity test (eo13920-supplier-test), Chinese-made or Chinese-owned units routed through these countries would still be covered, which makes enforcement and origin tracing an issue.

findings.entity: Mexico imports of 8504.23 (>10 MVA) from China
findings.claim: Mexico's own 2024 imports of >10 MVA liquid transformers (HS 8504.23) came mainly from China ($28.9M) and Spain ($27.8M), so routing large Chinese units through Mexico was small in 2024.
findings.detail: Mexican government data, collected by a sibling agent. This does not cover Chinese-owned plants that build in Mexico, which are unverified (see gaps).

findings.claim: CRS reports (Apr 23, 2026) that the US imports about 25-30% of its distribution transformers, mainly from Taiwan, Canada and Mexico. China is not named among the main sources.
findings.detail: This is consistent with China's displaced volume sitting in data-center MV, pad-mount and dry-type units (customer-owned, often bought outside utility channels) rather than in classic utility pole and pad-mount distribution.

findings.claim: Extra-high-voltage and large liquid transformers (8504.23) are in Annex III at a temporary 15% combined rate through Dec 31, 2027, while distribution transformers stay in Annex I-B at 25%.
findings.detail: From a Korean brokerage report. The White House Annex III PDF (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Annex-III.pdf) showed 8504.23.00, but the extraction was garbled. Non-Chinese replacements for sub-10 MVA Chinese units therefore pay 25%, versus 15% for >10 MVA, giving a domestic builder more tariff shelter in the sub-10 MVA segment.

findings.claim: Canada exported 15,568 small liquid transformers (≤650 kVA) worth $130.7M to the US in 2024, about $8,400 per unit.
findings.detail: Computed: $130,696k / 15,568 = $8,395. This is a lower anchor for unit values. No 8504.22 or 8504.23.0040 unit value was found for any origin.

gap_fill.analysis:
Coverage caveat: this run found no new primary data. All three WebSearch calls came back "budget used up", because the 200-call limit for this turn is shared by every agent in the workflow and other agents had already used it. As the tool instructed, I did not try a workaround. This output therefore reuses URL-backed results that sibling agents gathered earlier in this session, adds arithmetic reconciliation, and marks background-knowledge leads W. To finish the job, send a follow-up message, or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION, and run this domain first. The follow-up search plan table has the queries ready.

EO scope. The order number is still unresolved (eo-number-unresolved). The DOE RFI is FR Doc 2026-18370 (doe-rfi-citation), and rules are due around Dec 24, which is 120 days after signing (rules-due-date). Only the headline list of covered equipment is known (covered-equipment-headline). The 2026 RFI has the same title as EO 13920 (2020), which makes that order the likely template. If DOE reuses it, three things follow. The bulk-power system would cover equipment at 69 kV and above and exclude local distribution (eo13920-bps-definition). The supplier test would follow ownership, not factory location, so Chinese-owned plants in Mexico or the US would be caught (eo13920-supplier-test). Both points are unverified for the 2026 text.

The >8,000 vs 2.2% contradiction can be resolved with arithmetic. China shipped only about 50 units of 100 MVA or more in 2025 (china-share-gt100mva). If the 8,000 count covers Jan-Oct 2025, the units could not have averaged more than about $375k each even if all of China's $3.6B in HS 8504 shipments were transformers (reconcile-value-ceiling, china-8504-value). That is below every per-unit value found for imports above 10 MVA. So most of the 8,000 are units under 10 MVA: 8504.22 liquid pad-mount and unit-substation transformers, and 8504.34 dry-type. These are the data-center medium-voltage classes. This fits three other signals:
- WoodMac says China's share is near 30% only in "certain categories" (cnbc-30pct-categories).
- CRS says distribution imports come mainly from Taiwan, Canada and Mexico, not China (crs-distribution-imports).
- China's average export unit was about RMB205k (china-2025-unit-count).

Two caveats apply. WoodMac's definition is unpublished (woodmac-8000-definition), and the ">100 MVA" series may actually cover everything above 10 MVA (nextmsc-scope-risk). In 2026 China's US mix moved up into 10-220 MVA (goldman-2026-10-220), then fell 36% month on month in August (china-liquid-aug-na).

Size. At most about $7B of WoodMac's >$22B can be HS 8504, which includes inverters (woodmac-22b-mostly-non-transformer). The transformer displacement is worth single-digit billions, not $22B.

What this means for a builder:
- The overlap between what China actually supplied and what the EO probably covers is narrow. China's volume was concentrated below 10 MVA. Under a 13920-style definition those units fall outside scope unless DOE's rules reach customer-owned data-center substations.
- The 10-100 MVA units with high-voltage primaries are both likely covered and China's fastest-growing 2026 flow. That makes them the best target for 2027 demand.
- Sub-10 MVA units are a volume line with tariff shelter: 25% Section 232, versus 15% for units above 10 MVA (sec232-tiers). Demand there does not depend on the EO, and the segment is crowded.
- Hitachi Gallman (10-160 MVA) arrives in 2029 and VTC (2-500 MVA) in 2028. A new entrant would need to ship by 2028.
- Check the Dec 24 rules and JST's ownership before committing capital.
