findings.claim: This agent's own searches were all refused (shared 200-search budget exhausted). Every new finding below was re-extracted from search results that earlier agents in this session retrieved, and is attributed to the underlying URL.
findings.detail: The 'P' tag here only means the run status is certain. Several primary facts were read through search-engine summaries of primary PDFs (White House annexes, docket comments), not by opening the documents. Not covered: GOES imports by country, foreign GOES makers' US plans, Worthington/Tempel core capacity, a China GOES benchmark and Metglas capacity.

findings.claim: Imported laminations for stacked cores (HTS 8504.90.9634), stacked cores (8504.90.9638) and wound cores (8504.90.9642) are listed in Section 232 Annex I-B at 25% ad valorem on full customs value (June 2026 re-issue under Proclamation 11032).
findings.entity: Section 232 steel derivatives: transformer cores and laminations
findings.detail: This contradicts the dashboard row s232_cores (50%, x.com source, W). The April 2026 combined annex PDF (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/ANNEXES-I-A-I-B-II-III-IV.pdf) shows these codes under a heading titled '50%' but with a note saying 25%. That is probably a parsing artifact of the multi-annex file. I trust the standalone June Annex I-B. A product listed twice pays the rate once. Read through a search summary in the run-2 verify:dockets_policy agent. Confirm against CBP CSMS #68855869 and HTSUS chapter 99 before entry.

findings.claim: The Annex III temporary 15% list covers other transformer parts (8504.90.9646, .9650, .9690: 'parts for electrical transformers, nesoi, excluding laminations and cores'), so cores and laminations stay at 25% while most other transformer parts pay 15% combined through Dec 31, 2027.
findings.detail: Annex III also lists 8504.23.00 and 8504.34.00 (large liquid-filled units). AFS Law says Annex III items revert to the Annex I-B 25% after Dec 31, 2027 (https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/customs-import-compliance-blog/the-president-signs-proclamation-overhauling-section). Implication: an importer of large finished transformers pays 15% on the whole unit, while a domestic builder importing its cores pays 25% on the cores.

findings.claim: Imported GOES strip (HTS 7225.11.00 and 7226.11.10/.90.30/.90.60) is reported to pay 50% on full value as an Annex I-A chapter-72 article, but no source in this session showed those lines in the annex text.
findings.detail: The annex snippet confirms the Annex I-A rule ('a 50% ad valorem Section 232 tariff shall apply to the full value'), but the steel rows were truncated. Secondary commentary in the same results says the 50% tier applies to chapter 72 goods and that Annex I-A 'includes grain-oriented electrical steel'. tariffstool.com (W) gives MFN Free and Section 232 at 50% for 7225 (https://www.tariffstool.com/hts/alloy-steel-flat-7225). A MegaGrid vendor blog citing 'HS 7225.19' at 25% conflicts with the official sources and is discounted. Treat 50% as likely but unconfirmed.

findings.claim: If GOES strip pays 50% and cut cores pay 25%, imported cores beat imported strip whenever the core price per ton is below roughly 1.2 times the strip price plus 0.8 times the in-house cutting and scrap cost per ton (computed).
findings.detail: Derivation: strip route landed = 1.5*S + C; core route landed = 1.25*K; break-even K* = (1.5*S + C)/1.25 = 1.2*S + 0.8*C. Freight, MFN duty (reported Free) and scrap are ignored. Illustrations: with S = $3,190/t (GTAIC world import average, W), K* = $3,828/t + 0.8C; with S = $2,420/t (GTAIC Europe), K* = $2,904/t + 0.8C. This depends on goes-strip-232-50-unconfirmed. If strip is also 25%, the inversion disappears and K* = S + 0.8C. Section 232 applies to full value, so the foreign core maker's processing margin is also taxed at 25%.

findings.claim: CRS reports imported electrical 'steel articles' faced 50% tariffs from Aug 15, 2025, and that the administration removed country exemptions (Mexico, Canada, Australia) in Feb 2025. The dashboard's 50% on cores therefore describes the regime before Apr 6, 2026, not the current one.
findings.detail: This is a reconciliation, not a direct statement. CRS was published 17 days after Proclamation 11021 took effect and still cites 50%. I trust the June 2026 annex for the current rate. The pre-April regime applied the duty to metal content (from the baseline and background, not verified here). Cliffs' Nov 2, 2020 release title shows that GOES laminations and cores were first targeted by a 2020 Section 232 action (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20201102006028/en/Cleveland-Cliffs-Applauds-President-Trump%E2%80%99s-Actions-to-Address-Imports-of-Laminations-and-Cores-from-Electrical-Steel).

findings.claim: The Section 301 forced-labor duties (10% or 12.5%, from Jul 24, 2026) do not apply to articles subject to Section 232 steel, aluminum or copper headings (9903.82.02 and 9903.82.04-.26), so imported GOES strip and cores carry Section 232 duty only.
findings.entity: CBP CSMS 69326983 / USTR Section 301 forced-labor action
findings.detail: HTS list: https://content.govdelivery.com/attachments/USDHSCBP/2026/07/23/file_attachments/3723786/Forced%20Labor%20HTS%20LIST.pdf (exclusion heading 9903.05.90). The USTR fact sheet lists 'all articles and parts of articles subject to section 232 tariffs' as not covered. The baseline (market-map section 7) treats Section 301 as a 'small adder on Korean and Mexican imports'. For 8504 transformers that are Section 232 derivatives, that adder likely does not apply. Whether every 8504 line maps to the excluded 9903.82 headings is not verified line by line.

findings.claim: Proclamation 11032 (signed Jun 1, 2026, effective Jun 8, 2026; FR Doc 2026-11314, 91 FR 34085) re-issued the Section 232 annexes, added Annex I-C temporary rates, and expanded the 15% tier to agricultural equipment and some residential HVAC.
findings.detail: The 91 FR 34085 citation comes from the trade_flows domain's finding. Temporary changes run through Dec 31, 2027, then revert to Proclamation 11021 rates. No GOES-specific change surfaced in the results.

findings.claim: Unverified lead: Proclamation 11032 reportedly lowered the 'entirely American metal' threshold from 95% to 85%. That could let cores cut in Canada or Mexico from US-melted Cliffs GOES re-enter with reduced or no Section 232 duty.
findings.detail: Single W source (a blog). A second W page is titled 'Section 232 in 2026: 50% Rule, US Steel Exemption, and the 95% Content Threshold' (gingercontrol.com). If confirmed, a tolling model (Cliffs strip cut by a MX or CA core maker, cores back into the US) could beat both the 25% and 50% routes. Verify in the proclamation text and the CBP melt-and-pour guidance.

findings.claim: No source found a Japan, Korea, EU or UK country-specific Section 232 rate or quota for GOES or for cores. The Proclamation 11032 partner provisions found concern drawback eligibility for Annex I-B and III goods, plus a 15% combined cap on Annex I-C mobile equipment for 11 partners.
findings.detail: The Annex I-C cap comes from gingercontrol (W): https://gingercontrol.com/industries/industrial-machinery. The verifier concluded: 'I found no source saying EU or Japan were added to or removed from a transformer list.' Absence in search is not proof. Japan and Korea are the most likely GOES origins, so check the bilateral agreement texts.

findings.claim: DOE describes Cleveland-Cliffs Butler Works (Lyndora/Butler, PA) as the only US production facility for high-silicon grain-oriented electrical steel.
findings.detail: Zanesville Works OH has a Cliffs operations page (https://www.clevelandcliffs.com/operations/steelmaking/zanesville-works), but its GOES role and tonnage were not retrieved. Butler/Zanesville capacity in tons per year: NOT FOUND.

findings.claim: The $75M DOE support for Butler is the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations Industrial Demonstrations Program cost share (selected Mar 25, 2024; >$19M Phase 1 awarded Aug 2024) for four electric induction slab-reheat furnaces replacing two gas-fired ones, not new DPA Title III money.
findings.detail: This confirms the earlier unverified lead. The Butler Eagle (Oct 6, 2026) reports the grant passed Trump-administration review earlier in 2026 and was reframed from decarbonization to GOES output (https://www.butlereagle.com/20261006/feds-cleveland-cliffs-tout-200m-investment-in-butler-works/). BlueGreen Alliance dates the award Mar 25, 2024. Whether the $200M includes the $75M is still not explicit; the release says 'supported by'.

findings.claim: Cliffs' Oct 5, 2026 release puts Butler completion in early 2028. DOE's project page and Cliffs' SEC filings say 2029, and DOE's 2024 fact sheet targeted hot commissioning in Q2 2027 and completion in Q2 2028.
findings.detail: The Q2 2026 call also says 2028. I trust the newest company statement (early 2028) for timing, but plan around 2029 as the conservative case. Release date: Oct 5, 2026 per the verifier; the baseline says Oct 4. Furnaces are built in Warren, OH. About 220 construction jobs at peak (Butler Eagle).

findings.claim: Cliffs says the Butler project raises GOES production volume by up to 25%. DOE's 2024 materials cite a 12.5% increase in GOES shipments from better slab quality, and the tonnage base is undisclosed in every source.
findings.detail: A Cliffs SEC filing (Apr 2026, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764065/000076406526000054/clf-20260402.htm) is summarized as saying Cliffs wants '30% to 40% more tonnage of American-made GOES from existing capacity'. That came through a search summary, so treat it as S. The three figures may measure different things (volume vs shipments vs tonnage). Absolute tons per year: NOT FOUND.

findings.claim: Howard Industries told DOE (Jul 15, 2026) that Cliffs' Butler expansion targets GOES for power transformers, not distribution transformers, and called Cliffs' GOES capacity the real bottleneck.
findings.detail: Cliffs' own Q2 2026 call says the upgrade lets it 'supply more tons of high-end grain-oriented electrical steels' (https://www.clevelandcliffs.com/_assets/_c7d9d552b544a2a36f31808074ad8c21/clevelandcliffs/db/1111/12098/file/Q2+2026+Earnings+Call+Transcript.pdf). For a distribution-transformer entrant, that suggests little of the new volume will be lower-grade strip for non-captive distribution makers. Howard is a large incumbent buyer, so read this as its view. The attachment number of Howard's comment was not identified (candidates: 0004, 0015, 0022, 0023, 0032, 0033).

findings.claim: On Jul 1, 2026 Cliffs announced a contract with the Defense Logistics Agency / Department of War worth up to $400M for up to 53,000 short tons of Butler-made GOES over five years, through Sep 8, 2030.
findings.detail: Computed: $400M / 53,000 st = $7,547/st (about $8,319/t), a ceiling rather than a unit price. 53,000 / 5 = about 10,600 st/yr if spread evenly, a further claim on Butler output before the 2028 expansion. The baseline had no URL for this. Other coverage: yieh.com, indexbox, ssg.events. A primary-domain search (defense.gov, dla.mil, sam.gov) found no contract announcement.

findings.claim: Cleveland-Cliffs said on May 7, 2025 it would no longer deploy capital to the planned $150M Weirton, WV distribution-transformer plant, citing scope changes by its unnamed IP partner. Cliffs said it would still supply steel to that partner.
findings.detail: Corroborated by T&D World (https://www.tdworld.com/utility-business/article/55289293/cleveland-cliffs-pulls-plug-on-plan-to-build-west-virginia-transformer-plant), WTOV9 and Manufacturing Dive. Farm and Dairy gives May 2. The partner is planning its own plant. A 2026 search snippet citing 'Weirton expected online 1H 2026' repeats older filing language and is superseded. Baseline capacity_expansions.csv and market-map 2b should mark Weirton cancelled. So Cliffs is a supplier only, not a downstream competitor.

findings.claim: There is still no reliable US GOES transaction price. Public anchors range from about $3,892/short ton (a W tracker at $4.29/kg, Sep 2026) to a $7,547/short ton DLA contract ceiling. Cliffs' 2024 GOES raw-material surcharge was $375-465/net ton.
findings.detail: Computed: $4.29/kg x 907.185 = $3,892/st; surcharge $375-465/nt = $413-513/t. Other W anchors: IMARC says US electrical steel (not GOES-specific) reached $5,362/t in June (https://www.imarcgroup.com/electrical-steel-pricing-report). GTAIC average GOES import prices were $2.42k/t for Europe (Feb 2025-Jan 2026) and $3.19k/t for the world narrow definition (Apr 2025-Mar 2026), neither US-specific. Cliffs Q2 2026 average selling price across all steel was $1,124/nt (10-Q). No 2026 Cliffs GOES price-increase notice was found. The Fastmarkets China CRGO series (MB-STE-0952) exists but its value was not retrieved.

findings.claim: BLS publishes no PPI for grain-oriented or other electrical steel. The nearest proxy, cold-rolled steel sheet and strip (WPU101707), was 469.251 in Aug 2026, +27.6% since Nov 2025.
findings.detail: Computed: 469.251/367.621 - 1 = 27.6%. The value is 65.9% of the Nov 2021 peak (711.611, per Trading Economics). This is carbon cold-rolled sheet, only a sentiment proxy for GOES. Steel mill products (WPU1017) were 381.162 in Aug 2026.

findings.claim: CRS reports DOE found transformer price increases correlated with GOES price increases starting in 2021, and that BLS data show distribution and large power transformer prices up about 40% (inflation-adjusted) from 2020 to 2024. No source in this session confirmed the baseline's 'GOES doubled 2020-24'.
findings.detail: The 'doubled' figure still rests only on Breakthrough Journal [S]. The source of DOE's underlying GOES price series (rulemaking TSD or CRS footnote 63) was not retrieved.

findings.claim: DOE's Feb 2022 grid supply-chain review found the single US GOES maker could not meet domestic demand for the highest-quality steel at prices comparable to imported GOES.
findings.entity: DOE 2022 Electric Grid Supply Chain Review
findings.detail: This supports the baseline's grade gap. The ~920mm Cliffs width limit (vs >=932mm wanted) is still sourced only to Breakthrough [S]; no Cliffs spec sheet surfaced.

findings.claim: CRS, citing a Commerce study, reports US imports of finished transformer cores rose from $29M in 2016 to $205M in 2019 (2024 dollars), with Mexico and Canada supplying roughly 95% of the 2019 total.
findings.detail: Computed: about 7.1x growth over 2016-2019. This shows an established North American merchant core supply in MX and CA (relevant to Worthington/Tempel). Data for 2020-2026 and tonnage/unit values were not found. CRS also says the US imports 25-30% of distribution transformers, mainly from Taiwan, Canada and Mexico.

findings.claim: DOE's Jun 15, 2026 RFI (FR Doc 2026-11971, docket EERE-2026-BT-STD-0133, comments due Jul 15, 2026) asks how the April 2024 standards affect national security, core-manufacturing capacity and surge production. It notes some classes could be met by moving to amorphous cores. Compliance applies from Apr 23, 2029.
findings.detail: The RFI was triggered by Presidential Determination 2026-10. It asks about the availability, lead times and constraints of distribution-transformer core manufacturing, foreign-sourcing reliance and regulatory flexibilities. Several commenters cite 'May 2029'; DOE's page says Apr 23, 2029. The Federal Register files the notice as a 'proposed rule' type, but its content is an RFI.

findings.claim: As of the latest search (early Oct 2026), no NOPR, compliance delay or withdrawal of the 2024 distribution-transformer standard had appeared on federalregister.gov, energy.gov or reginfo.gov after the Jul 15, 2026 comment close.
findings.detail: This is a negative finding from search, not proof of absence. Next check: the OIRA review queue on reginfo.gov. EPCA's six-year lookback after the April 2024 final rule points to about 2030 for the next mandatory determination or NOPR. The rule stands unless DOE acts. EPCA's anti-backsliding provision (cited by NEMA) limits weakening the levels, so a compliance-date delay is likelier than a rollback; that is my inference.

findings.claim: In July 2026 comments, EEI supported the 2024 rule but asked for longer compliance time; APPA sought no changes but urged monitoring of amorphous supply; NRECA said the rule 'strikes the right balance'; NEMA urged certainty; Cleveland-Cliffs (Jul 15) supported changes to preserve GOES for all covered distribution transformers.
findings.detail: This sources the baseline's previously unlinked 'EEI wants a later compliance date'. EEI's requested date is not stated. Other filers: ERMCO (Jul 13) calls the rule 'reasonable, balanced, and achievable'; SCE (Jul 14) raises amorphous supply-chain risk; individual Denny Wist favors delay. Cliffs' CEO framing: Butler Eagle Aug 7, 2026 (https://www.butlereagle.com/20260807/cliffs-ceo-says-grain-oriented-steel-essential-as-dept-of-energy-mulls-2024-transformer-ruling/). Utility Dive also says the 2024 final rule required less amorphous steel than the 2023 proposal and added two years to compliance.

findings.claim: NEMA's Jul 15, 2026 comment says the US has a single domestic GOES producer and that the only large-scale amorphous steel producer supplies just 2% of the entire distribution-transformer market.
findings.detail: NEMA also backs Section 3 of H.R. 4626, which would remove distribution transformers from the EPCA review schedule. NEMA does not name the producer; Metglas/Proterial in Conway SC is the presumed one, not verified. Metglas capacity and expansion: NOT FOUND (search returned nothing relevant). If the 2029 levels push some classes to amorphous, a supplier now serving about 2% of the market is a single-source bottleneck.

findings.claim: Howard Industries' comment says it has committed more than $180M of capital tied to the 2024 rule ($30M at Laurel MS, $50M elsewhere), that most transformer lead times are now under 20 weeks with some under 10, and that it should be reimbursed if DOE changes the rule.
findings.detail: This conflicts with the baseline's distribution lead times (pad-mount 30-60 weeks, pole 26-40 weeks, from W trackers). Howard is an interested party arguing that supply has recovered, and 'most transformer' lead times probably means its own product mix. I trust it as a datapoint on an incumbent's own lead times, not as a market average. Still, a filed statement from the largest domestic distribution maker that lead times are under 20 weeks is a meaningful bearish signal for a new distribution entrant.

findings.claim: The House passed H.R. 4626 (Home Appliance Protection and Affordability Act); APPA reports it would bar new distribution-transformer efficiency standards and future changes to them.
findings.detail: Senate status and the passage date were not found. NEMA supports Section 3. If enacted, it would freeze the 2024 levels (the April 2029 compliance would presumably stand) and remove the risk of further tightening; that is my inference.

findings.claim: CRS reports that Hitachi Energy imports amorphous steel from China for its Quebec plant, and a docket commenter says China and South Korea are subsidizing domestic amorphous steel and distribution-transformer production.
findings.detail: No volume or tariff treatment was found for amorphous ribbon (likely HTS 7226.99 or 7225.xx; not verified). For a US entrant, China-sourced ribbon is the obvious alternative to Metglas but carries Section 232 and foreign-adversary policy risk.

findings.claim: A July 2026 docket comment estimates that about 80% of GOES used in the US is imported; this is an unverified commenter estimate.
findings.detail: It surfaced in a search summary alongside DPA material. The commenter is not identified. No USITC/Census series for HTS 7225.11/7226.11 by country (2024-2026) was obtained, so origins and volumes remain NOT FOUND.

findings.claim: Presidential Determination 2026-10 (Apr 20, 2026) was published at 91 FR 21931 on Apr 23, 2026, and federalregister.gov lists it as FR Doc 2026-08013. The baseline cites 2026-08011, which may be a different determination published the same day.
findings.detail: A W analysis (grantedai.com) reports a $323M FY2026 DPA authorization and a Sep 30, 2026 Title III sunset absent reauthorization. No DPA Title III award, purchase commitment or funding notice for GOES or cores was found on energy.gov, grants.gov or sam.gov.

gap_fill.analysis:
Coverage caveat: this agent's own searches were refused because the session's 200-search budget was spent. Every new item was re-extracted from search results that earlier agents in this session had already retrieved, and is cited to the underlying URL. Several primary facts were read through search summaries of primary PDFs (run-status-reused-results).

1. Tariffs now favor importing finished cores over importing strip.
- Laminations, stacked cores and wound cores (8504.90.9634/.9638/.9642) are in Annex I-B at 25% of full value (cores-232-annexIB-25). They are explicitly left off the temporary 15% Annex III list (cores-excluded-annexIII). The dashboard's 50% reflects the regime before Apr 6, 2026 (cores-50pct-pre-april-regime).
- GOES strip is reported at 50% under Annex I-A, but the line was not seen in the annex text (goes-strip-232-50-unconfirmed).
- If 50% holds, imported cores win whenever their price is below about 1.2x the strip price plus 0.8x the in-house cutting cost (tariff-inversion-breakeven).
- Section 301 forced-labor duties do not stack on either, because Section 232 articles are excluded (s301-excludes-232-articles). The same exclusion likely removes the baseline's 301 adder on 232-covered transformer imports.
- No Japan, Korea, EU or UK carve-out for GOES or cores was found (no-country-deal-goes).
- A W-sourced lead: cores cut in Mexico or Canada from US-melted Cliffs strip might enter at a reduced rate under the 85% US-metal threshold (us-metal-threshold-lead).

2. Domestic strip relief comes late and is probably not aimed at distribution grades.
- Butler is still the only US GOES facility (cliffs-butler-only-facility).
- Its expansion is a 2024 OCED decarbonization grant that was re-framed as a GOES-output project, not new DPA money (cliffs-butler-award-origin, dpa-pd-fr-citation).
- Completion is early 2028 per Cliffs and 2029 per DOE and the filings (cliffs-butler-timing). Output gains are +25% per Cliffs or +12.5% per DOE, with no tonnage base disclosed (cliffs-butler-output).
- Howard says the new volume targets power-transformer grades (howard-butler-power-grades).
- Defense demand claims up to 53,000 short tons over five years (dla-goes-contract).
- Cliffs exited the Weirton transformer plant (weirton-cancelled), so it is a supplier, not a competitor, but it has no reason to give a newcomer allocation.
- Mexico and Canada already dominated merchant core imports (core-imports-value). A non-captive entrant should plan on bought-in North American cores at 25% until at least 2028.

3. Price visibility is poor.
- There is no GOES PPI (no-goes-ppi).
- The anchors span about 2x: roughly $3,900/st (a W tracker) to a $7,547/st DLA ceiling (goes-price-anchors).
- The baseline's 'GOES doubled 2020-24' remains single-sourced (goes-transformer-price-link).
- Model GOES as an unhedgeable pass-through, and quote with steel escalators.

4. The 2029 rule has not moved.
- No NOPR or delay appeared after the Jul 15 close (doe-no-followup-after-rfi). Compliance stays Apr 23, 2029 (doe-rfi-scope).
- Utilities, NEMA, Howard and ERMCO back the rule, and EEI wants more time. Only Cliffs seeks changes (doe-docket-positions).
- NEMA says the one large-scale amorphous producer supplies about 2% of the market (nema-amorphous-2pct). Chinese ribbon is the alternative, and it carries policy risk (amorphous-china-quebec). A House-passed bill could freeze the standards (hr4626-epca-exemption).

Plant-design implication:
- Design around bought-in GOES stacked and wound cores.
- Keep an amorphous wound-core option for the classes the 2029 levels push there.
- Do not build a strip slitting/cutting line until the 7225.11 rate and any US-metal tolling route are confirmed.

A cautionary signal: Howard's filed claim that its lead times are under 20 weeks (howard-comment-leadtimes) suggests distribution supply is loosening faster than the baseline shows.
